title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: Rostov had come to Tilsit on the worst possible day for delivering a petition on Denisov's behalf. He couldn't go to the general himself, being in civilian clothes and having come to Tilsit without permission; and Boris, even had he wanted to, couldn't have done anything the following day either. On that day — June 27 — the peace preliminaries were signed. The Emperors exchanged decorations: Alexander received the Cross of the Legion of Honor and Napoleon the Order of Saint Andrew of the First Degree. A dinner had been arranged for that evening, given by a battalion of the French Guards for the Preobrazhensky battalion. The Emperors were to attend.

Rostov felt so ill at ease with Boris that when Boris looked in after supper, he pretended to be asleep. Early the next morning he left, avoiding Boris. In civilian clothes and a round hat, he wandered through the town, staring at the French and their uniforms and at the streets and buildings where the Russian and French Emperors were staying. In a square he saw tables being set up and preparations underway for the dinner; he saw Russian and French flags draped across the streets with huge monograms A and N. The windows of the houses also displayed flags and bunting.

"Boris doesn't want to help me, and I don't want to ask him. That's settled," Nicholas thought. "It's all over between us, but I won't leave without doing everything I can for Denisov — and certainly not without getting his letter to the Emperor. The Emperor! He's right here!" thought Rostov, who had unconsciously wandered back to the house where Alexander was staying.
Saddled horses stood before the building and the suite was assembling, evidently preparing for the Emperor to come out.

"I could see him at any moment," thought Rostov. "If only I could hand the letter to him directly and tell him everything... Would they really arrest me for being in civilian clothes? Surely not! He would understand who is in the right. He understands everything, knows everything. Who could be more just, more generous than he? And even if they did arrest me for being here — what would it matter?" he thought, looking at an officer entering the Emperor's residence. "People go in all the time. It's all nonsense! I'll go in and give the letter to the Emperor myself — so much the worse for Drubetskoy, who's driven me to it!" And with a resolve that surprised even himself, Rostov felt for the letter in his pocket and went straight to the house.

"No — I won't miss my chance this time, the way I did after Austerlitz," he thought, expecting at any moment to encounter the sovereign and feeling the blood rush to his heart at the thought. "I'll fall at his feet and beg him. He'll raise me up, listen, and even thank me. 'I am happy when I can do good, but to right an injustice is the greatest happiness,'" Rostov imagined the sovereign saying. And ignoring the curious stares of passersby, he entered the porch of the Emperor's residence.
A broad staircase led straight up from the entrance, and to the right he saw a closed door. Below, under the staircase, was a door to the lower floor.
"Whom do you want?" someone asked.
"To deliver a letter — a petition — to His Majesty," said Nicholas, his voice trembling.
"A petition? This way, to the officer on duty" — he was shown the door leading downstairs — "only it won't be accepted."

Hearing this indifferent voice, Rostov was struck with fear at what he was doing. The thought of encountering the Emperor at any moment was thrilling and therefore terrifying, and he was ready to bolt. But the official who had questioned him opened the door, and Rostov walked in.

A short, stocky man of about thirty, in white breeches, high boots, and a fine batiste shirt he had obviously just put on, stood in the room while his valet buttoned a new pair of handsome silk-embroidered suspenders onto the back of his breeches — which, for some reason, caught Rostov's attention. This man was speaking to someone in the next room.
"A good figure and in her first bloom," he was saying — but on seeing Rostov, he stopped and frowned.
"What is it? A petition?"
"What is it?" asked the person in the other room.
"Another petitioner," answered the man with the suspenders.
"Tell him to come back later. He'll be coming out soon — we need to go."
"Later... later! Tomorrow. It's too late..."
Rostov turned to leave, but the man in the suspenders stopped him.
"Who sent you? Who are you?"
"I come from Major Denisov," answered Rostov.
"Are you an officer?"
"Lieutenant Count Rostov."
"What nerve! Submit it through your commander. Now get along with you — go!" And he went back to putting on the uniform his valet was handing him.
Rostov went back into the hall and realized that the porch was now crowded with officers and generals in full dress uniform, through whom he had to pass.

Cursing his own audacity, his heart sinking at the thought of coming face to face with the Emperor and being humiliated and arrested in his presence — fully aware now of how improper his conduct was and regretting it — Rostov, with downcast eyes, was making his way out through the glittering suite when a familiar voice called him and a hand seized his arm.
"What are you doing here in civilian dress, sir?" asked a deep voice.
It was a cavalry general who had earned the Emperor's special favor during this campaign and who had previously commanded the division in which Rostov served.

Rostov began stammering an excuse, but seeing the general's kind, good-humored face, he pulled him aside and in an excited voice told him the whole story, begging him to intercede for Denisov, whom the general knew. After hearing him out, the general shook his head gravely.
"I'm sorry — sorry for the fine fellow. Give me the letter."

Barely had Rostov handed over the letter and finished explaining Denisov's case when hurried footsteps and the jingle of spurs were heard on the stairs, and the general, leaving him, went to the porch. The gentlemen of the Emperor's suite ran down the stairs to their horses. Hayne, the same groom who had been at Austerlitz, led up the Emperor's horse, and the faint creak of a footstep Rostov recognized at once sounded on the stairs. Forgetting the danger of being recognized, Rostov moved close to the porch with some curious civilians, and once again — after two years — he saw the features he adored: the same face, the same gaze, the same step, the same blend of majesty and gentleness. The feeling of enthusiasm and love for his sovereign rose again in Rostov's soul with all its old force. In his Preobrazhensky uniform — white leather breeches and high boots — wearing a star Rostov didn't recognize (it was the Legion of Honor), the sovereign came out onto the porch, pulling on his gloves and carrying his hat under his arm. He paused, looked around, and his glance seemed to brighten everything it touched. He spoke a few words to some generals, and recognizing the former commander of Rostov's division, smiled and beckoned him over.
The whole suite drew back, and Rostov saw the general talking with the Emperor for some time.

The Emperor said a few words and then stepped toward his horse. Again the crowd of courtiers and onlookers (Rostov among them) moved closer. Stopping beside his horse with one hand on the saddle, the Emperor turned to the cavalry general and said in a loud voice, clearly intending to be heard by all:
"I cannot do it, General. I cannot — because the law is stronger than I." And he put his foot in the stirrup.
The general bowed respectfully, and the sovereign mounted and rode off down the street at a gallop. Beside himself with emotion, Rostov ran after him with the crowd.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: The Emperor rode to the square where a battalion of the Preobrazhensky regiment stood on one side, facing a battalion of the French Guards in their bearskin caps on the other.

As the Tsar approached one end of the line, another group of horsemen galloped up from the opposite direction, and at their head Rostov recognized Napoleon. It could be no one else. He came at a gallop wearing a small hat, a blue uniform open over a white vest, and the Saint Andrew ribbon across his shoulder. He rode a superb gray Arab horse with a crimson, gold-embroidered saddlecloth. Approaching Alexander, he raised his hat, and as he did so, Rostov — with his cavalryman's eye — couldn't help noticing that Napoleon didn't sit well or firmly in the saddle. The battalions shouted "Hurrah!" and "Vive l'Empereur!" Napoleon said something to Alexander, and both Emperors dismounted and took each other's hands. Napoleon's face wore an unpleasant, artificial smile. Alexander was saying something pleasant to him.

Despite the trampling of the French gendarmes' horses, which were pushing back the crowd, Rostov kept his eyes on every movement of both Alexander and Bonaparte. He was struck to see Alexander treating Bonaparte as an equal, and that Napoleon was completely at ease with the Tsar, as though such encounters with an Emperor were an everyday matter for him.

Alexander and Napoleon, with their long trains of attendants, approached the right side of the Preobrazhensky battalion and came straight up to the crowd. The crowd unexpectedly found itself so close to the Emperors that Rostov, standing in the front row, was afraid he might be recognized.
"Sire, I ask your permission to present the Legion of Honor to the bravest of your soldiers," said a sharp, precise voice, articulating every letter.
It was the short Napoleon, looking straight up into Alexander's eyes. Alexander listened attentively, then bent his head and smiled pleasantly.

"To the one who bore himself most bravely in this last war," Napoleon added, emphasizing each syllable, and with a composure that irritated Rostov, he ran his eyes over the Russian ranks drawn up before him — every soldier standing at attention, eyes fixed on their Emperor.
"Will Your Majesty allow me to consult the colonel?" said Alexander, and he took a few quick steps toward Prince Kozlovski, the battalion commander.
Meanwhile, Bonaparte began pulling the glove off his small white hand, tore it in the process, and threw it away. An aide-de-camp behind him scrambled to pick it up.
"To whom shall it be given?" Emperor Alexander asked Kozlovski in Russian, in a low voice.
"To whomever Your Majesty commands."
The Emperor knit his brows with displeasure and, glancing back, remarked:
"But we must give him an answer."
Kozlovski scanned the ranks with a resolute eye, and his gaze swept over Rostov.
"Can it be me?" thought Rostov.
"Lazarev!" the colonel called, frowning, and Lazarev, the first soldier in the rank, stepped briskly forward.

"Where are you going? Stay here!" voices whispered to Lazarev, who didn't know where to go. He stopped, casting an anxious sidelong glance at his colonel. His face twitched, as often happens to soldiers called before the ranks.

Napoleon slightly turned his head and reached his plump little hand behind him, as if to take something. His suite, instantly guessing what he wanted, whispered and passed something from hand to hand, and a page — the same one Rostov had seen the night before at Boris's — ran forward, bowed respectfully over the outstretched hand, and without a moment's delay placed an Order on a red ribbon into it. Napoleon, without looking, pressed two fingers together and held the medal between them. Then he approached Lazarev — who kept rolling his eyes and staring stubbornly at his own sovereign — glanced at Emperor Alexander as if to say that what he was about to do was done for the sake of his ally, and his small white hand, holding the Order, touched one of Lazarev's buttons. It was as if Napoleon knew that the mere touch of his hand on this soldier's chest would make the man forever happy, singled out from all the rest of humanity. Napoleon simply laid the cross on Lazarev's breast and, dropping his hand, turned toward Alexander — certain the cross would stay in place. And it did.

Eager hands — Russian and French — immediately seized the medal and pinned it to the uniform. Lazarev glanced sullenly at the little man with white hands who was doing something to him, and still standing motionless at attention, looked straight at Alexander again — as if asking whether he should stay there, or leave, or do something else. But receiving no orders, he remained frozen in that rigid position for some time.
The Emperors remounted and rode away. The Preobrazhensky battalion broke ranks and mingled with the French Guards, and they sat down together at the tables that had been prepared.

Lazarev sat in the place of honor. Russian and French officers embraced him, congratulated him, and shook his hand. Crowds of officers and civilians gathered just to look at him. A hum of Russian and French voices and laughter filled the square around the tables. Two officers with flushed, happy faces walked past Rostov.
"What do you think of the feast? All on silver plate!" one of them was saying. "Have you seen Lazarev?"
"I have."
"Tomorrow, I hear, the Preobrazhenskis are hosting the French."
"Yes, but what luck for Lazarev! Twelve hundred francs a year for life."
"Here's a cap, boys!" shouted a Preobrazhensky soldier, pulling on a shaggy French cap.
"That's a fine thing! First-rate!"

"Have you heard the password?" one Guards officer asked another. "The day before yesterday it was 'Napoleon, France, bravoure'; yesterday, 'Alexandre, Russie, grandeur.' One day our Emperor gives it, the next day Napoleon. Tomorrow our Emperor will send a Saint George's Cross to the bravest of the French Guards. Has to be done — he must reciprocate."
Boris, together with his friend Zhilinski, also came to watch the Preobrazhensky banquet. On his way back he spotted Rostov standing by the corner of a building.
"Rostov! How are you? We missed each other," he said — and couldn't help asking what was wrong, so strangely gloomy and troubled was Rostov's face.
"Nothing, nothing," Rostov replied.
"You'll come by?"
"Yes, I will."

Rostov stood at that corner for a long time, watching the feast from afar. A painful process was working itself out in his mind, one he couldn't bring to a conclusion. Terrible doubts rose in his soul. He remembered Denisov with his altered expression, his submission, and the whole hospital — arms and legs torn off, filth and disease. So vividly did he recall the hospital stench of dead flesh that he looked around to find where the smell was coming from. Then he thought of that self-satisfied Bonaparte with his small white hands, who was now an Emperor — liked and respected by Alexander. Then why the severed limbs and the dead? Then his mind jumped to Lazarev rewarded while Denisov was punished and unforgiven. He caught himself thinking such strange thoughts that he frightened himself.

The smell of the food the Preobrazhenskis were eating and a pang of hunger brought him back. He had to eat something before leaving. He went to a hotel he had noticed that morning. He found it so packed with people — including officers who, like himself, had come in civilian clothes — that he could barely get a table. Two officers from his own division joined him. The conversation naturally turned to the peace. The officers, like most of the army, were unhappy with the peace concluded after Friedland. They said if Russia had held out a bit longer, Napoleon would have been finished — his troops had neither food nor ammunition. Nicholas ate and drank (mainly drank) in silence. He finished two bottles of wine by himself. The process in his mind went on tormenting him without reaching resolution. He feared to give in to his thoughts, yet couldn't shake them. Suddenly, when one of the officers said it was humiliating to look at the French, Rostov erupted with an uncalled-for fury that startled everyone:
"How can you judge what's best?" he cried, blood rushing to his face. "How can you judge the Emperor's actions? What right do we have to argue? We can't comprehend the Emperor's aims or his actions!"
"But I never said anything about the Emperor!" said the officer, defending himself, unable to explain Rostov's outburst except by assuming he was drunk.
But Rostov wasn't listening.

"We're not diplomats — we're soldiers, nothing more," he went on. "If we're ordered to die, we die. If we're punished, it means we deserve it. It's not for us to judge. If the Emperor sees fit to recognize Bonaparte as Emperor and make an alliance with him, then that's the right thing to do. If we start judging and arguing about everything, nothing will be sacred! Next we'll be saying there is no God — nothing!" shouted Nicholas, banging the table — very little to the point as far as his listeners could tell, but perfectly relevant to the train of his own thoughts.
"Our job is to do our duty — to fight, not to think! That's all," he said.
"And to drink," said one of the officers, not wanting a quarrel.
"Yes, and to drink," Nicholas agreed. "Hey there! Another bottle!" he shouted.
In 1808 Emperor Alexander went to Erfurt for another meeting with Emperor Napoleon, and in the upper circles of Petersburg there was much talk of the grandeur of this important occasion.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: In 1809, the intimacy between "the world's two arbiters," as Napoleon and Alexander were called, had become so close that when Napoleon declared war on Austria, a Russian corps crossed the frontier to fight alongside their old enemy Bonaparte against their old ally the Austrian Emperor, and at court people even spoke of a possible marriage between Napoleon and one of Alexander's sisters. But besides foreign policy, Russian society's attention was keenly focused on the internal reforms being carried out across all branches of government.

Life, meanwhile — real life, with its essential concerns of health and sickness, work and rest, and its intellectual pursuits of thought, science, poetry, music, love, friendship, hatred, and passion — went on as usual, independently of and apart from political friendship or enmity with Napoleon Bonaparte, and from all the grand schemes of reform.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Next morning, having said goodbye to no one but the count and without waiting for the ladies to appear, Prince Andrew set off for home.

It was already the beginning of June when, on his return journey, he drove into the birch forest where the gnarled old oak had made such a strange and memorable impression on him. In the forest the harness bells sounded even more muffled than they had six weeks before, for now everything was thick, shady, and dense. The young firs scattered through the forest no longer clashed with the general beauty but, blending in with the mood around them, were delicately green with fluffy new shoots.

The whole day had been hot. Somewhere a storm was gathering, but only a small cloud had sprinkled a few raindrops on the road and the juicy leaves. The left side of the forest was dark in shadow; the right side sparkled in the sunlight, wet and glistening and barely stirred by the breeze. Everything was in bloom, the nightingales trilled, and their songs echoed now near, now far away.

"Yes — it was here in this forest, with that oak I agreed with," thought Prince Andrew. "But where is it?" he wondered again, looking to the left side of the road, and without recognizing it, he gazed in admiration at the very oak he had been looking for. The old oak, completely transformed, spread a canopy of rich, dark-green foliage and stood swaying gently, almost trembling, in the rays of the evening sun. Neither gnarled fingers nor old scars nor old doubts and sorrows were anywhere in evidence. Through the tough, century-old bark — even where there were no branches — leaves had sprouted, so fresh and vigorous it was hard to believe the old veteran could have produced them.

"Yes, it is the same oak," thought Prince Andrew, and all at once he was seized by an unreasoning springtime feeling of joy and renewal. All the best moments of his life suddenly rose to his memory. Austerlitz with the vast heavens, his wife's dead, reproachful face, Pierre at the ferry, that girl thrilled by the beauty of the night, and that night itself, and the moon — all of it rushed suddenly into his mind.

"No, life is not over at thirty-one!" Prince Andrew suddenly decided, finally and irrevocably. "It's not enough for me to know what I have inside me — everyone must know it: Pierre, and that young girl who wanted to fly into the sky — everyone must know me, so that my life is not lived for myself alone, apart from everyone else, but so that it is reflected in them all, and they and I may live in harmony!"

On reaching home, Prince Andrew decided to go to Petersburg that autumn and found all sorts of reasons to justify this decision. A whole series of sensible, logical arguments showing that it was essential to go — and even to re-enter the service — kept springing up in his mind. He could not now understand how he had ever doubted the necessity of taking an active part in life, just as a month ago he hadn't understood how the idea of leaving the country could enter his head. It now seemed clear that all his experience of life would be senselessly wasted unless he put it to some use and played an active role again. He didn't even remember how, on the strength of similar flimsy logic, it had previously seemed obvious that he'd be debasing himself if he allowed himself — after the lessons life had taught him — to believe again in the possibility of being useful, and in the possibility of happiness or love. Now reason pointed in exactly the opposite direction. After that trip to Ryazan he found country life dull; his old pursuits no longer interested him, and often, sitting alone in his study, he would get up, go to the mirror, and stare at his own face for a long time. Then he would turn away to look at the portrait of his dead Lise, who, with her hair curled a la grecque, gazed out of the gilt frame tenderly and cheerfully. She no longer spoke those terrible words to him but simply looked at him — merrily, curiously, and questioningly. And Prince Andrew, clasping his hands behind his back, would pace the room for ages, now frowning, now smiling, as he pondered those irrational, inexpressible thoughts — secret as a crime — that altered his entire life and were connected with Pierre, with fame, with the girl at the window, the oak, and woman's beauty and love. And if anyone came into his room at such moments, he was particularly cold, stern, and above all unpleasantly logical.
"My dear," Princess Mary would say, entering at such a moment, "little Nicholas can't go out today — it's very cold."

"If it were hot," Prince Andrew would reply at such times very drily to his sister, "he could go out in his smock. But since it's cold, he must wear warm clothes, which were designed for that purpose. That is the logical consequence of it being cold — not that a child who needs fresh air should be kept indoors." He would add this with exaggerated logic, as if punishing someone for those secret, illogical emotions stirring within him.
At such moments Princess Mary would think how intellectual work dries men up.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Prince Andrew arrived in Petersburg in August 1809. It was the time when the young Speransky was at the peak of his fame and his reforms were being pushed forward with the greatest energy. That same August, the Emperor was thrown from his carriage, injured his leg, and spent three weeks at Peterhof, receiving Speransky every day and no one else. At that time the two famous decrees were being prepared that so agitated society — abolishing court ranks and requiring examinations for the grades of Collegiate Assessor and State Councilor — and not just these, but a whole state constitution intended to transform the existing system of government in Russia: legal, administrative, and financial, from the Council of State down to the district courts. Now those vague liberal dreams with which Emperor Alexander had ascended the throne, and which he had tried to realize with the help of his associates Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Kochubey, and Strogonov — whom he himself jokingly called his Comite de salut public — were taking concrete shape.

Now all these men had been replaced by Speransky on the civilian side and Arakcheev on the military. Soon after his arrival, Prince Andrew — as a gentleman of the chamber — presented himself at court and at a levee. The Emperor, though he saw him twice, did not favor him with a single word. It had always seemed to Prince Andrew that he was antipathetic to the Emperor, that the sovereign disliked his face and personality — and in the cold, distant glance Alexander gave him, he found further confirmation. The courtiers explained the Emperor's neglect as displeasure at Bolkonski's not having served since 1805.

"I know perfectly well that one can't help one's sympathies and antipathies," thought Prince Andrew, "so there's no point presenting my proposal for army reform to the Emperor personally. The project will speak for itself."

He mentioned what he had written to an old field marshal who was a friend of his father's. The field marshal gave him an appointment, received him graciously, and promised to inform the Emperor. A few days later, Prince Andrew received notice that he was to see the Minister of War, Count Arakcheev.
On the appointed day, Prince Andrew entered Count Arakcheev's waiting room at nine in the morning.
He didn't know Arakcheev personally, had never seen him, and everything he'd heard about the man inspired little respect.

"He is the Minister of War, a man trusted by the Emperor — I needn't concern myself with his personal qualities. He's been asked to review my project, and he alone can get it approved," thought Prince Andrew as he waited among various important and unimportant people in Arakcheev's anteroom.

During his time as an aide-de-camp, Prince Andrew had seen the waiting rooms of many powerful men and knew the different types well. Arakcheev's anteroom had a very distinctive character. The faces of the minor petitioners showed embarrassment and servility; the faces of those of higher rank wore a shared expression of unease, masked by an air of indifference and ironic self-mockery directed at themselves, their situation, and the person they were waiting to see. Some paced thoughtfully; others whispered and laughed. Prince Andrew heard the nickname "Sila Andreevich" and the words "Uncle will give it to us hot" — in reference to Arakcheev. One general, an important person, was clearly offended at having to wait so long and sat crossing and uncrossing his legs, smiling contemptuously to himself.

But the moment the door opened, every face showed one expression only: fear. Prince Andrew asked the duty adjutant a second time to announce him, but received an ironic look and was told his turn would come. After several others had been shown in and out of the minister's office, an officer entered whose humiliated, frightened manner struck Prince Andrew. This man's audience lasted a long time. Then suddenly a harsh, grating voice was heard from behind the door, and the officer — pale-faced and trembling — came out through the waiting room, clutching his head.
After this, Prince Andrew was led to the door, and the duty officer whispered: "To the right, by the window."

Prince Andrew entered a plain, tidy room and saw at the table a man of about forty with a long torso, a long close-cropped head, deep wrinkles, scowling brows above dull greenish-hazel eyes, and a large, overhanging red nose. Arakcheev turned his head toward him without actually looking at him.
"What is your petition?" asked Arakcheev.
"I am not petitioning, your excellency," Prince Andrew replied quietly.
Arakcheev's eyes turned toward him.
"Sit down," he said. "Prince Bolkonski?"
"I'm not petitioning for anything. His Majesty the Emperor has been pleased to send your excellency a project I submitted..."

"You see, my dear sir, I have read your project," Arakcheev interrupted, beginning amiably enough but then — again without looking at Prince Andrew — gradually lapsing into a tone of grumbling contempt. "You are proposing new military laws? There are plenty of laws already, but no one to enforce the old ones. Nowadays everyone designs laws — it's easier to write than to act."
"I came at His Majesty the Emperor's wish to learn how your excellency proposes to deal with the memorandum I submitted," said Prince Andrew politely.

"I have written my comments on your memorandum and forwarded it to the committee. I do not approve of it," said Arakcheev, standing up and taking a paper from his desk. "Here!" And he handed it to Prince Andrew.

Scrawled across the paper in pencil, without capitals, misspelled, and without punctuation, was: "unsoundly constructed because resembles an imitation of the french military code and from the articles of war needlessly deviating."
"To which committee has the memorandum been referred?" asked Prince Andrew.
"To the Committee on Army Regulations. And I have recommended that your honor be appointed a member — but without salary."
Prince Andrew smiled.
"I don't want one."
"A member without salary," repeated Arakcheev. "I have the honor... Well! Call the next one! Who else is there?" he shouted, bowing Prince Andrew out.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: While waiting for his committee appointment, Prince Andrew looked up his old acquaintances, particularly those he knew to be in power and whose help he might need. In Petersburg he now felt what he had felt on the eve of battle: a troubled curiosity, an irresistible pull toward the ruling circles where the future — on which the fate of millions depended — was being shaped. From the irritation of older officials, the curiosity of outsiders, the discretion of insiders, the hurry and preoccupation of everyone, and the countless committees and commissions he heard about daily, he sensed that here in Petersburg in 1809, a vast civic battle was being prepared — one whose commander in chief was a mysterious figure he didn't know but who was said to be a genius: Speransky. And this reform movement, which Prince Andrew understood only vaguely, with Speransky as its chief driver, began to interest him so intensely that the question of army regulations quickly receded to second place in his mind.

Prince Andrew was ideally positioned to gain entry to the highest and most varied Petersburg circles. The reforming party welcomed and courted him — first because he was reputed to be clever and exceptionally well-read, and second because by freeing his serfs he had earned a reputation as a liberal. The old guard, who disapproved of the innovations, turned to him expecting sympathy, simply because he was his father's son. Fashionable society welcomed him gladly because he was rich, distinguished, a good match, and almost a newcomer with a halo of romance from his supposed death and the tragic loss of his wife. Besides all this, the general view of everyone who had known him before was that he had greatly improved over the past five years — softened, become more mature, lost his old affectation, pride, and contemptuous irony, and gained the calm that comes with age. People talked about him, were interested in him, and wanted to meet him.

The day after his interview with Arakcheev, Prince Andrew spent the evening at Count Kochubey's. He told the count about his meeting with "Sila Andreevich" — Kochubey used that nickname with the same vague irony Prince Andrew had noticed in the War Minister's waiting room.
"My dear friend, even in this matter you can't get by without Michael Mikhailovich Speransky. He manages everything. I'll speak to him. He's promised to come this evening."
"What does Speransky have to do with army regulations?" asked Prince Andrew.
Kochubey shook his head with a knowing smile, as if surprised by Bolkonski's naivety.
"We were talking about you with him just the other day," Kochubey continued, "and about your freed serfs."
"Oh, so it's you, Prince, who've freed your serfs?" said an old man of Catherine's era, turning contemptuously toward Bolkonski.
"It was a small estate that brought in no income," replied Prince Andrew, trying to downplay his action so as not to needlessly irritate the old man.
"Afraid of being late..." said the old man, glancing at Kochubey.

"There's one thing I don't understand," he went on. "Who will plow the land if they're set free? It's easy to write laws but hard to govern. It's the same as now — I ask you, Count — who'll run the departments when everyone has to pass examinations?"
"Those who pass the examinations, I suppose," replied Kochubey, crossing his legs and looking around.
"Well, I have Pryanichnikov serving under me — a splendid man, a priceless man — but he's sixty. Is he supposed to take an examination?"
"Yes, that's a difficulty, since education is not yet widespread, but..."

Count Kochubey didn't finish. He stood up, took Prince Andrew's arm, and went to meet a tall, bald, fair-haired man of about forty, with a large open forehead and a long face of unusual, peculiar whiteness, who was just entering. The newcomer wore a blue tailcoat with a cross on a ribbon around his neck and a star on his left breast. It was Speransky. Prince Andrew recognized him at once and felt a throb within him — as happens at critical moments of life. Whether it was respect, envy, or anticipation, he couldn't tell. Speransky's whole figure was of a distinctive type that made him instantly recognizable. In the society Prince Andrew frequented, he had never encountered anyone who combined such awkward, clumsy gestures with such calm self-possession; he had never seen such a resolute yet gentle expression as that in those half-closed, slightly moist eyes, or so firm a smile that expressed nothing in particular; nor had he heard such a refined, smooth, soft voice. Above all, he had never seen such delicate whiteness of face and hands — broad hands, but very plump, soft, and white. Such whiteness and softness Prince Andrew had only seen on the faces of soldiers who had been in the hospital a long time. This was Speransky, Secretary of State, the Emperor's reporter, and his companion at Erfurt, where he had met and talked with Napoleon more than once.

Speransky did not shift his gaze from face to face as people instinctively do when entering a large gathering, and was in no hurry to speak. He spoke slowly, confident he would be listened to, and looked only at the person he was addressing.

Prince Andrew followed Speransky's every word and gesture with particular attention. As sometimes happens — especially with people who judge those around them harshly — whenever he met someone new, especially someone he knew by reputation, like Speransky, he expected to discover in him the perfection of human qualities.

Speransky told Kochubey he was sorry he couldn't come sooner — he'd been held up at the palace. He didn't say the Emperor had detained him, and Prince Andrew noticed this affectation of modesty. When Kochubey introduced him, Speransky slowly turned his gaze to Bolkonski with his customary smile and looked at him in silence.
"I am very glad to make your acquaintance. I've heard of you, as everyone has," he said after a pause.
Kochubey said a few words about Arakcheev's reception of Bolkonski. Speransky smiled more noticeably.

"The chairman of the Army Regulations Committee is my good friend Monsieur Magnitsky," he said, fully articulating every word and syllable, "and if you like, I can put you in touch with him." He paused at the period. "I hope you will find him open-minded and ready to support everything reasonable."
A circle quickly formed around Speransky, and the old man who had talked about his subordinate Pryanichnikov addressed a question to him.

Prince Andrew, without joining the conversation, watched Speransky's every move — this man who not long ago had been an insignificant seminary student and now, Bolkonski thought, held in his plump white hands the fate of Russia. Prince Andrew was struck by the extraordinary disdainful composure with which Speransky answered the old man. He seemed to be addressing condescending words to him from an immeasurable height. When the old man started talking too loudly, Speransky smiled and said he couldn't judge the merits of what pleased the sovereign.
After chatting briefly in the general circle, Speransky rose and came up to Prince Andrew, taking him to the far end of the room. It was clear he thought it worth cultivating Bolkonski.

"I had no chance to talk with you, Prince, during that lively exchange the venerable gentleman drew me into," he said, with a slightly contemptuous smile that seemed to say: "You and I both understand how insignificant those people are." This flattered Prince Andrew. "I've known of you for some time — first from your liberation of your serfs, a pioneering example that deserves many more imitators, and second because you are one of those gentlemen of the chamber who have not taken offense at the new decree regarding court ranks, which is causing so much gossip and indignation."
"No," said Prince Andrew, "my father did not want me to take advantage of that privilege. I began my service from the lowest grade."
"Your father — a man of the previous century — evidently stands above our contemporaries who so condemn a measure that merely restores natural justice."

"I think, however, that these objections have some basis," said Prince Andrew, trying to resist Speransky's influence, which he was beginning to feel. He didn't want to agree with him on everything and felt a need to push back. Though he usually spoke easily and well, he found it hard to express himself now while talking with Speransky — he was too absorbed in studying the famous man's personality.
"Grounds of personal ambition, perhaps," Speransky said quietly.
"And of state interest, to some extent," said Prince Andrew.
"What do you mean?" asked Speransky softly, lowering his eyes.

"I am an admirer of Montesquieu," replied Prince Andrew, "and his idea that the principle of monarchies is honor strikes me as indisputable. Certain rights and privileges of the nobility seem to me a means of sustaining that sentiment."
"The principle of monarchies is honor seems to me incontestable. Certain rights and privileges for the aristocracy appear to me a means of maintaining that sentiment."
The smile vanished from Speransky's white face, which was much improved by the change. Apparently Prince Andrew's thought genuinely interested him.
"If you look at the question from that angle..." he began, pronouncing French with visible difficulty and speaking even more slowly than in Russian but quite calmly.
"If you regard the question from that point of view."

Speransky went on to say that honor — l'honneur — cannot be upheld by privileges that harm the state; that honor is either a negative concept of refraining from what is blameworthy, or it is a source of emulation in the pursuit of commendation and rewards. His arguments were concise, simple, and clear.

"An institution that upholds honor as a source of emulation — something like the Legion of Honor established by the great Emperor Napoleon — is not harmful but helpful to the success of the service, and is not a class or court privilege."

"I don't dispute that, but it cannot be denied that court privileges have served the same purpose," Prince Andrew responded. "Every courtier considers himself bound to maintain his position with dignity."

"Yet you yourself haven't chosen to avail yourself of the privilege, Prince," said Speransky, indicating by a smile that he wished to end amiably a discussion that was becoming uncomfortable for his companion. "If you would do me the honor of calling on Wednesday," he added, "I will have spoken with Magnitsky by then and can tell you what may interest you. I would also welcome the chance for a more extended conversation."
Closing his eyes, he gave a French-style bow without saying goodbye and, trying to draw as little attention as possible, left the room.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: During the first weeks of his stay in Petersburg, Prince Andrew felt the entire framework of thought he had built during his secluded country life overshadowed by the trivial demands that engulfed him in the city.

Returning home each evening, he would jot down four or five necessary calls or appointments in his notebook. The mechanics of daily life — arranging his schedule so as to be everywhere on time — absorbed most of his vital energy. He did nothing, didn't even think or find time to think, but only talked — and talked successfully — about what he had thought about while in the country.

He sometimes noticed with annoyance that he repeated the same remark on the same day in different circles. But he was so busy from morning to night that he had no time to notice he was thinking about nothing.

As at their first meeting at Kochubey's, Speransky made a powerful impression on Prince Andrew when he received him privately at his own house on Wednesday and talked to him at length and in confidence.

To Bolkonski, so many people seemed contemptible and insignificant, and he so longed to find in someone the living ideal of perfection toward which he strived, that he readily believed he had found this ideal in Speransky — a perfectly rational and virtuous man. Had Speransky come from the same class and had the same breeding and traditions, Bolkonski would quickly have discovered his weak, human, unheroic sides. But Speransky's strange, logical turn of mind inspired a respect that was all the greater because he didn't fully understand the man. Moreover, Speransky — whether because he genuinely appreciated the other's abilities or because he considered it necessary to win him over — showed off his dispassionate, calm rationality before Prince Andrew and flattered him with that subtle flattery that goes hand in hand with self-confidence: the tacit assumption that one's companion is the only other person besides oneself capable of seeing the foolishness of the rest of mankind and the reasonableness of one's own ideas.

During their long conversation on Wednesday evening, Speransky said more than once: "We look at everything that rises above the common level of established custom..." or, with a smile: "But we want the wolves fed and the sheep safe..." or: "They can't understand this..." — all in a way that seemed to say: "We — you and I — understand what they are and who we are."

This first long conversation with Speransky only deepened in Prince Andrew the feeling he had had at their first encounter. He saw in him a remarkable, clear-thinking man of vast intellect who, through energy and persistence, had attained power — and who was using it solely for Russia's good. In Prince Andrew's eyes, Speransky was the man he himself would have wished to be: one who could account rationally for every fact of life, who considered only what was rational to be important, and who could apply the standard of reason to everything. Everything seemed so simple and clear in Speransky's presentation that Prince Andrew found himself agreeing on every point. If he argued back, it was only to maintain his independence and not submit to Speransky's views entirely. Everything was right and as it should be — with one exception that troubled Prince Andrew: Speransky's cold, mirrorlike gaze, which didn't let you see into his soul, and his delicate white hands, which Prince Andrew kept watching involuntarily, the way one watches the hands of those who hold power. That mirrorlike look and those soft hands irritated Prince Andrew, though he didn't know why. He was also unpleasantly struck by the excessive contempt for others he observed in Speransky, and by the variety of logical maneuvers he used to support his positions. He deployed every kind of mental tool except analogy, and shifted too boldly, Prince Andrew felt, from one mode to another. At one moment he would take the stance of a practical man and dismiss dreamers; then he would become a satirist, laughing ironically at his opponents; then he would grow severely logical; then suddenly soar into the realm of metaphysics. (This last tactic he used very frequently.) He would elevate a question to metaphysical heights, jump to definitions of space, time, and thought, and having extracted the rebuttal he needed, would descend again to the original level of discussion.

In general, what struck Prince Andrew most about Speransky's mind was his absolute, unshakable faith in the power and authority of reason. It was clear that the thought which to Prince Andrew seemed so natural — namely, that everything one thinks and believes might ultimately be nonsense — could never occur to Speransky. And it was precisely this trait that especially attracted Prince Andrew.

During the first period of their acquaintance, Bolkonski felt a passionate admiration for Speransky similar to what he had once felt for Bonaparte. The fact that Speransky was the son of a village priest, and that petty people might despise him for his humble origins (as many did), only made Prince Andrew cherish this feeling more and unconsciously reinforce it.

That first evening, Bolkonski mentioned the Commission for the Revision of the Legal Code. Speransky told him sardonically that the Commission had existed for 150 years, had cost millions, and had accomplished nothing — except that Rosenkampf had stuck labels on the corresponding paragraphs of the different codes.

"And that is all the state has to show for the millions it spent," he said. "We want to give the Senate new judicial powers, but we have no laws. That is why it's a sin for men like you, Prince, not to be serving in times like these!"
Prince Andrew said that such work required a legal education he did not have.
"But nobody has it, so what would you have? It's a vicious circle, and we must break out of it."

A week later, Prince Andrew was a member of the Committee on Army Regulations and — what he hadn't expected at all — chairman of a section of the commission for revising the legal code. At Speransky's request, he took on the first part of the Civil Code being drafted and, using the Napoleonic Code and the Institutes of Justinian, began working on the section on Personal Rights.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Nearly two years earlier, in 1808, Pierre had returned to Petersburg from his estates and found himself involuntarily thrust into a leading role among the city's Freemasons. He organized dinner meetings and funeral lodge gatherings, enrolled new members, and worked to unite various lodges and obtain authentic charters. He donated money for the construction of temples and made up the shortfall in charitable contributions, which most members were stingy and irregular about paying. He almost single-handedly supported a poorhouse the Order had founded in Petersburg.

His own life, meanwhile, continued as before — the same indulgences and dissipations. He liked to eat and drink well, and though he considered it immoral and degrading, he could not resist the temptations of the bachelor circles in which he moved.

Amid the whirl of his activities and distractions, however, Pierre began to feel — by the end of a year — that the more firmly he tried to stand on the ground of Masonry, the more it gave way beneath him. At the same time, he felt that the deeper it sank, the more inextricably bound he became to the Order. When he first joined the Freemasons, he had felt like a man confidently stepping onto what looks like the smooth surface of a bog. When he put one foot down, it sank. To make sure of the ground, he put the other foot down — and sank deeper. And now he was stuck, wading knee-deep in the mire whether he liked it or not.

Joseph Alexeevich was not in Petersburg — he had lately withdrawn from the affairs of the Petersburg lodges and lived almost entirely in Moscow. All the lodge members were men Pierre knew in ordinary life, and it was hard for him to see them merely as Brothers in Freemasonry rather than as Prince B. or Ivan Vasilevich D., whom he knew socially as weak and unimpressive men. Beneath the Masonic aprons and insignia, he saw the mundane uniforms and medals they coveted in real life. Often, after collecting dues and tallying the twenty or thirty rubles received — mostly in promises — from a dozen members, half of whom could pay as easily as he could, Pierre remembered the Masonic vow in which each Brother pledged to devote all his worldly goods to his neighbor. Doubts he tried to suppress kept rising in his soul.

He divided the Brothers he knew into four categories. In the first he placed those who took no active part in the affairs of the lodges or in the world, but were exclusively occupied with the mystical science of the Order — questions about the threefold name of God, the three primordial elements (sulphur, mercury, and salt), or the meaning of the square and the various symbols of Solomon's temple. Pierre respected this class — to which the senior members mostly belonged, including, he believed, Joseph Alexeevich himself — but he didn't share their interests. His heart wasn't in the mystical side of Freemasonry.
In the second category he placed himself and others like him — seekers and doubters who hadn't yet found a clear, direct path in Freemasonry but hoped to.

In the third he put those Brothers (the majority) who saw nothing in Freemasonry but its outward forms and ceremonies and valued their strict performance without caring about their meaning or purpose. Willarski and even the Grand Master of the principal lodge belonged to this group.

Finally, the fourth category — also very large — consisted of men who believed in nothing and wanted nothing, but joined the Freemasons simply to associate with the wealthy young brothers who were influential through their connections or rank, and of whom there were a great many in the lodge.

Pierre began to feel dissatisfied with what he was doing. Freemasonry — at least as he experienced it — sometimes seemed to him based on nothing but outward show. He didn't dream of doubting Freemasonry itself, but suspected that Russian Masonry had taken a wrong turn and departed from its original principles. And so, toward the end of the year, he went abroad to be initiated into the Order's higher mysteries.

In the summer of 1809, Pierre returned to Petersburg. The Russian Freemasons, who had learned through correspondence with their foreign counterparts that Bezukhov had gained the trust of many highly placed individuals, had been initiated into numerous secrets, had been elevated to a higher degree, and was bringing back much that could benefit the Masonic cause in Russia — all came to see him, tried to win his favor, and seemed to believe he was preparing something for them while keeping it to himself.

A solemn meeting of the second-degree lodge was convened, at which Pierre promised to share with the Petersburg Brothers what he had been charged to deliver from the Order's highest leaders. The hall was full. After the customary rituals, Pierre stood and began his address.

"Dear Brothers," he began, blushing and stammering, a written speech in his hand, "it is not enough to observe our mysteries in the seclusion of our lodge — we must act — act! We are asleep, but we must act." Pierre raised his notebook and began to read.

"For the spread of pure truth and the triumph of virtue," he read, "we must cleanse men of prejudice, promote principles in harmony with the spirit of the times, undertake the education of the young, unite ourselves in unbreakable bonds with the wisest men, and boldly yet prudently combat superstition, unbelief, and folly, forming from those devoted to us a body linked by common purpose and possessing authority and power.

"To this end, we must secure the dominance of virtue over vice and strive to ensure that the honest man may, even in this world, receive a lasting reward for his goodness. But in these great efforts we are gravely hampered by the political institutions of today. What is to be done? Favor revolutions? Overthrow everything? Repel force by force? No! We are far from that. Every violent reform deserves condemnation, for it cannot remedy evil while men remain what they are, and because wisdom has no need of violence.

"The entire plan of our Order should be grounded in the idea of cultivating men of strength and virtue, bound by shared conviction, whose purpose is to punish vice and folly, patronize talent and goodness, and raise worthy men from obscurity into our Brotherhood. Only then will our Order have the power to quietly restrain the supporters of disorder and control them without their even knowing it. In a word, we must establish a form of government with universal reach, spread across the whole world, without dissolving the bonds of citizenship — one alongside which all other governments can continue as usual in everything except what impedes the great aim of our Order: to secure the victory of virtue over vice. This was Christianity's own aim. It taught men to be wise and good and, for their own benefit, to follow the example and instruction of the best and wisest men.

"In those times, when everything was plunged in darkness, preaching alone was naturally enough. The novelty of Truth gave her special power. But now we need far stronger methods. It is now necessary that man, governed by his senses, should find in virtue something tangible and attractive to those senses. It is impossible to uproot the passions; but we must strive to direct them toward noble ends, and therefore everyone must be able to satisfy his passions within the bounds of virtue. Our Order should provide the means for this.

"As soon as we have a certain number of worthy men in every country, each training two others, all closely united — everything will be possible for our Order, which has already accomplished much in secret for the good of mankind."

This speech not only made a strong impression but caused a stir in the lodge. The majority of Brothers, seeing in it the dangerous ideas of Illuminism, received it with a coldness that surprised Pierre. The Grand Master began to reply, and Pierre defended his views with growing passion. It had been a long time since there had been so heated a meeting. Factions formed — some accusing Pierre of Illuminism, others supporting him. At that meeting, Pierre was struck for the first time by the infinite variety of human minds, which makes it impossible for a truth to present itself the same way to any two people. Even those who seemed to be on his side understood him in their own way, with reservations and modifications he couldn't accept — since what he wanted most of all was to convey his thoughts to others exactly as he understood them himself.
The Illuminati sought to replace monarchical institutions with republican ones.

At the end of the meeting, the Grand Master rebuked Bezukhov — with irony and ill will — for his vehemence, saying it was not only a love of virtue but also a love of argument that had driven him. Pierre did not respond, and asked simply whether his proposal would be accepted. He was told it would not. Without waiting for the usual formalities, he left the lodge and went home.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Once again Pierre was overtaken by the depression he dreaded so much. For three days after delivering his speech at the lodge, he lay on a sofa at home, seeing no one and going nowhere.
It was just then that he received a letter from his wife, who begged him to see her, telling him how upset she was about him and how she wished to devote her whole life to him.
At the end of the letter she informed him that she would be returning to Petersburg from abroad in a few days.

Shortly after this letter, one of the Masonic Brothers whom Pierre respected less than the others forced his way in to see him. Turning the conversation to Pierre's marriage, he offered some brotherly advice, suggesting that Pierre's harshness toward his wife was wrong and that he was violating one of the fundamental rules of Freemasonry by refusing to forgive the repentant.

At the same time his mother-in-law, Prince Vasili's wife, sent word begging him to come, if only for a few minutes, to discuss an extremely important matter. Pierre could see there was a conspiracy against him and that they wanted to reunite him with his wife, but in his current state of mind, this wasn't even unpleasant to him. Nothing mattered to him. Nothing in life seemed particularly important, and under the weight of the depression that gripped him, he valued neither his freedom nor his determination to punish his wife.
"No one is right and no one is to blame; so she too is not to blame," he thought.

If he didn't immediately agree to a reunion with his wife, it was only because in his depressed state he didn't feel capable of taking any step at all. Had his wife simply come to him, he wouldn't have turned her away. Compared to what was preoccupying him, did it really matter whether he lived with his wife or not?
Without replying to either his wife or his mother-in-law, Pierre set out late one night for Moscow to see Joseph Alexeevich. This is what he wrote in his diary:
Moscow, 17th November

I have just returned from my benefactor and hasten to write down what I experienced. Joseph Alexeevich is living in poverty and has been suffering for three years from a painful bladder disease. No one has ever heard him groan or utter a word of complaint. From morning till late at night, except when he eats his very plain food, he works on his studies. He received me warmly and had me sit on the bed where he lay. I made the sign of the Knights of the East and of Jerusalem, and he responded in kind, asking me with a gentle smile what I had learned and gained in the Prussian and Scottish lodges. I told him everything as best I could, including what I had proposed to our Petersburg lodge, the poor reception I had met with, and my break with the Brothers. Joseph Alexeevich, after remaining silent and thoughtful for a long while, shared his view of the matter, which immediately illuminated my entire past and the future path I should follow. He surprised me by asking whether I remembered the threefold aim of the order: (1) The preservation and study of the mystery. (2) The purification and reformation of oneself for its reception, and (3) The improvement of the human race by striving for such purification. Which is the principal aim of these three? Certainly self-reformation and self-purification. Only toward this aim can we always strive, regardless of circumstances. But at the same time, this very aim demands the greatest efforts from us; and so, led astray by pride, losing sight of this aim, we occupy ourselves either with the mystery — which in our impurity we are unworthy to receive — or seek to reform the human race while ourselves setting an example of baseness and depravity. Illuminism is not a pure doctrine, precisely because it is attracted to social activism and inflated by pride. On these grounds Joseph Alexeevich condemned my speech and my entire course of action, and in the depths of my soul I agreed with him. Speaking of my family affairs he said to me: "The chief duty of a true Mason, as I have told you, lies in perfecting himself. We often think that by removing all the difficulties from our lives we will reach our goal more quickly, but on the contrary, my dear sir, it is only in the midst of worldly cares that we can achieve our three chief aims: (1) Self-knowledge — for man can only know himself through comparison, (2) Self-perfecting, which can only be attained through struggle, and (3) The attainment of the chief virtue — love of death. Only the trials of life can reveal its vanity and nurture our innate love of death, or of rebirth to a new life." These words are all the more remarkable because, despite his great physical suffering, Joseph Alexeevich never tires of life, though he loves death — for which, in spite of the purity and loftiness of his inner being, he does not yet feel himself sufficiently prepared. My benefactor then explained to me in full the meaning of the Great Square of creation and pointed out that the numbers three and seven are the foundation of everything. He advised me not to withdraw from the Petersburg Brothers, but to take only second-rank positions in the lodge, and to try, while steering the Brothers away from pride, to turn them toward the true path of self-knowledge and self-perfecting. Besides this, he advised me personally above all to keep watch over myself, and to that end he gave me a notebook — the one I am now writing in — in which I will henceforth record all my actions.
Petersburg, 23rd November

I am living with my wife again. My mother-in-law came to me in tears and said that Helene was here and begged me to hear her; that she was innocent and miserable at my desertion, and much more. I knew that if I once let myself see her I wouldn't have the strength to keep refusing what she wanted. In my confusion I didn't know whose aid or advice to seek. Had my benefactor been here he would have told me what to do. I went to my room and reread Joseph Alexeevich's letters and recalled my conversations with him, and from all of it concluded that I must not refuse someone who comes asking for help, and must extend a hand to everyone — especially to one so closely bound to me — and that I must bear my cross. But if I forgive her for the sake of doing right, then let our reunion serve only a spiritual purpose. That is what I decided, and what I wrote to Joseph Alexeevich. I told my wife that I asked her to forget the past, to forgive me whatever wrong I may have done her, and that I had nothing to forgive. It gave me joy to tell her this. She need not know how hard it was for me to see her again. I have settled on the upper floor of this big house and am feeling a happy sense of renewal.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: At that time, as always happens, the highest society — the circles that gathered at court and at the grand balls — was divided into several groups, each with its own particular character. The largest of these was the French circle allied with Napoleon, the circle of Count Rumyantsev and Caulaincourt. In this group Helene, as soon as she had settled in Petersburg with her husband, took a very prominent place. She was visited by members of the French embassy and by many people known for their intelligence and polished manners.

Helene had been at Erfurt during the famous meeting of the Emperors and had brought back from there her connections with Napoleonic dignitaries. At Erfurt her success had been brilliant. Napoleon himself had noticed her in the theater and said of her: "That's a superb creature." Her success as a beautiful and elegant woman did not surprise Pierre, for she had become even more attractive than before. What did surprise him was that during these last two years his wife had somehow acquired the reputation of being as charming and witty as she was beautiful. The distinguished Prince de Ligne wrote her eight-page letters. Bilibin saved up his best witticisms to deliver them in Countess Bezukhova's presence. To be received in the Countess Bezukhova's salon was considered a mark of intellectual distinction. Young men read books before attending Helene's evenings so they would have something to say in her salon, and secretaries of the embassy, and even ambassadors, confided diplomatic secrets to her, so that in a way Helene became a force. Pierre, who knew she was very stupid, sometimes attended her evenings and dinner parties — where politics, poetry, and philosophy were discussed — with a strange feeling of bewilderment and dread. At these parties he felt like a conjurer who always expects his trick to be found out. But whether because stupidity was exactly what was needed to run such a salon, or because the people being deceived found pleasure in the deception, the illusion was never exposed, and Helene Bezukhova's reputation as a lovely and clever woman became so firmly established that she could say the emptiest and most foolish things and everybody would go into raptures over every word, finding deep meaning in it that she herself never intended.
* "That's a superb creature."
* (2) "A charming woman, as witty as she is beautiful."

Pierre was exactly the kind of husband a brilliant society woman needed. He was that absent-minded eccentric, a grand nobleman of a husband who was in nobody's way and who, far from lowering the tone of the drawing room, actually enhanced it — his very contrast with his wife making her appear to better advantage. Pierre, during the last two years, as a result of his constant absorption in abstract matters and his genuine indifference to everything else, had acquired in his wife's circle — which held no interest for him — that air of ease, detachment, and goodwill toward all that cannot be faked and therefore commands real respect. He entered his wife's drawing room as one enters a theater: he knew everyone, was equally glad to see everyone, and equally indifferent to them all. Sometimes he joined in a conversation that interested him and, regardless of whether any important diplomats were present, would share his views in his slightly lisping way — views that were sometimes completely at odds with the prevailing tone. But the general opinion of the eccentric husband of "the most distinguished woman in Petersburg" was so well established that no one took his quirks seriously.

Among the many young men who visited the house every day, Boris Drubetskoy — who had already achieved considerable success in the service — was the most intimate friend of the Bezukhov household since Helene's return from Erfurt. Helene called him "my page" and treated him like a child. Her smile for him was the same as for everyone, but sometimes that smile made Pierre uncomfortable. Toward Pierre, Boris behaved with a particularly dignified and mournful deference. This shade of deference also disturbed Pierre. He had suffered so painfully three years before from the humiliation his wife had put him through that he now protected himself from any repeat, first by not being a husband to his wife in any real sense, and second by refusing to allow himself to suspect anything.

"No, now that she's become an intellectual she has finally given up her old infatuations," he told himself. "There has never been a case of a bluestocking having love affairs" — a statement which, though he'd picked it up from somewhere unknown, he believed completely. Yet strangely, Boris's constant presence in his wife's drawing room had a physical effect on Pierre: it made him stiff, constrained, and robbed him of his natural ease of movement.
"What a strange dislike," thought Pierre, "and yet I used to be quite fond of him."

In the eyes of the world Pierre was a great nobleman, the somewhat blind and foolish husband of a distinguished wife, a clever eccentric who did nothing and harmed nobody and was a thoroughly good-natured fellow. But a complex and difficult process of inner transformation was taking place all this time in Pierre's soul, revealing much to him and causing him both spiritual anguish and joy.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Pierre continued with his diary, and this is what he wrote during that time:
24th November

Got up at eight, read the Scriptures, then went to my duties. (On Joseph Alexeevich's advice, Pierre had entered government service and was working on one of the committees.) Came home for dinner and dined alone — the countess had many visitors I don't care for. I ate and drank in moderation and after dinner copied out some passages for the Brothers. In the evening I went down to the countess and told a funny story about B., and only remembered afterwards that I shouldn't have done so when everybody burst out laughing.

I am going to bed with a happy and peaceful mind. Great God, help me to walk in Your ways: (1) to conquer anger through calm and deliberation, (2) to overcome lust through self-discipline and repulsion, (3) to withdraw from worldliness, but not to avoid (a) the service of the state, (b) family duties, (c) relations with friends, and the management of my affairs.
27th November

I got up late. On waking I lay in bed a long time, giving in to laziness. O God, help and strengthen me that I may walk in Your ways! Read the Scriptures, but without proper feeling. Brother Urusov came and we talked about worldly vanities. He told me about the Emperor's new projects. I began to criticize them, but remembered my rules and my benefactor's words — that a true Freemason should be a zealous worker for the state when his help is needed, and a quiet observer when not called upon to assist. My tongue is my enemy. Brothers G. V. and O. visited me and we had a preliminary talk about admitting a new Brother. They assigned me the duty of Rhetor. I feel weak and unworthy. Then our talk turned to interpreting the seven pillars and steps of the Temple, the seven sciences, the seven virtues, the seven vices, and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Brother O. was very eloquent. In the evening the admission took place. The new decoration of the premises added much to the magnificence of the spectacle. It was Boris Drubetskoy who was admitted. I nominated him and served as Rhetor. A strange feeling stirred in me the whole time I stood alone with him in the dark chamber. I caught myself harboring a feeling of hatred toward him which I tried in vain to overcome. That is exactly why I would like to save him from evil and lead him onto the path of truth, but ill thoughts of him would not leave me. It seemed to me that his purpose in joining the Brotherhood was merely to grow close to and win favor with members of our lodge. Apart from the fact that he had asked me several times whether N. and S. were members of our lodge (a question I could not answer), and that, by my observation, he is incapable of feeling any real respect for our holy order and is too absorbed in and satisfied with outward appearances to desire spiritual improvement, I had no real cause to doubt him — yet he struck me as insincere, and the whole time I stood alone with him in the dark temple, it seemed to me he was smiling contemptuously at my words, and I truly wanted to plunge the sword I held to his bare chest. I could not summon eloquence, nor could I frankly voice my doubts to the Brothers and the Grand Master. Great Architect of Nature, help me find the true path out of this labyrinth of lies!
After this, three pages were left blank in the diary, and then the following was written:

I had a long and instructive conversation alone with Brother V., who advised me to hold fast by Brother A. Though I am unworthy, much was revealed to me. Adonai is the name of the creator of the world. Elohim is the name of the ruler of all. The third name is the unutterable name which means the All. Conversations with Brother V. strengthen, refresh, and support me on the path of virtue. In his presence doubt has no place. The distinction between the shallow teachings of worldly science and our sacred all-embracing teaching is clear to me. Human sciences dissect everything to understand it, and kill everything to examine it. In the holy science of our order all is one, all is known in its completeness and life. The Trinity — the three elements of matter — are sulphur, mercury, and salt. Sulphur is of an oily and fiery nature; in combination with salt, by its fiery nature it arouses a desire in the latter by means of which it attracts mercury, seizes it, holds it, and in combination produces other substances. Mercury is a fluid, volatile, spiritual essence. Christ, the Holy Spirit, Him!...
3rd December

Woke late, read the Scriptures but felt listless. Afterward went and paced up and down the large hall. I wanted to meditate, but instead my imagination kept picturing something that happened four years ago, when Dolokhov ran into me in Moscow after our duel and said he hoped I was enjoying perfect peace of mind despite my wife's absence. At the time I gave him no answer. Now I recalled every detail of that encounter and in my mind gave him the most vicious and bitter replies. I caught myself and pushed the thought away only when I realized I was burning with anger — but I didn't repent enough. Then Boris Drubetskoy came and began telling various stories. His visit irritated me from the start, and I said something unpleasant to him. He responded. I flared up and said much that was rude and even cruel to him. He fell silent, and I came to my senses only when it was too late. My God, I cannot get along with him at all. The cause of this is my own selfishness. I set myself above him and so become much worse than he, for he is patient with my rudeness while I on the contrary harbor contempt for him. O God, grant that in his presence I may see my own failings, and behave so that he too may benefit. After dinner I fell asleep, and as I was dozing off I clearly heard a voice in my left ear saying: "Your day!"

I dreamed I was walking in the dark and was suddenly surrounded by dogs, but I went on without fear. Suddenly a small dog seized my left thigh with its teeth and wouldn't let go. I began to choke it with my hands. No sooner had I torn it off than another, bigger one, began biting me. I lifted it up, but the higher I lifted it the bigger and heavier it grew. Then Brother A. appeared and, taking my arm, led me to a building we could only enter by walking along a narrow plank. I stepped on it, but it bent and gave way and I began to climb a fence I could barely reach with my hands. After much effort I dragged myself up, so that my leg hung down on one side and my body on the other. I looked around and saw Brother A. standing on the fence, pointing me toward a broad avenue and garden, and in the garden was a large and beautiful building. I woke up. O Lord, great Architect of Nature, help me to tear from myself these dogs — my passions, especially the last, which combines in itself the strength of all the others — and help me enter that temple of virtue which I glimpsed in my dream.
7th December

I dreamed that Joseph Alexeevich was sitting in my house, and that I was very glad and wanted to make him welcome. It seemed as if I was chattering endlessly with other people and suddenly remembered that this could not please him, and I wished to go close to him and embrace him. But as soon as I drew near, I saw that his face had changed and grown young, and he was quietly telling me something about the teachings of our order, but so softly that I couldn't hear. Then it seemed we all left the room and something strange happened. We were sitting or lying on the floor. He was telling me something, and I wished to show him my sensitivity, and not listening to what he was saying I began imagining the state of my inner man and the grace of God sanctifying me. Tears came to my eyes, and I was glad he noticed. But he looked at me with annoyance and jumped up, breaking off his remarks. I felt ashamed and asked whether what he'd been saying didn't concern me; but he didn't reply, gave me a kind look, and then we suddenly found ourselves in my bedroom where there is a double bed. He lay down on the edge of it and I burned with longing to be close to him and lie down too. And he said: "Tell me honestly, what is your chief temptation? Do you know it? I think you know it already." Embarrassed by this question, I answered that laziness was my chief temptation. He shook his head in disbelief; and even more ashamed, I said that though I was living with my wife as he had advised, I was not living with her as her husband. To this he replied that one should not deprive a wife of one's embraces, and gave me to understand that that was my duty. But I answered that I would be ashamed to do it, and suddenly everything vanished. I woke up and found in my mind the text from the Gospel: "The life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." Joseph Alexeevich's face had looked young and bright. That day I received a letter from my benefactor in which he wrote about "conjugal duties."
9th December

I had a dream from which I awoke with a pounding heart. I saw that I was in Moscow in my house, in the large sitting room, and Joseph Alexeevich came in from the drawing room. I seemed to know at once that the process of spiritual renewal had already taken place in him, and I rushed to meet him. I embraced him and kissed his hands, and he said: "Have you noticed that my face is different?" I looked at him, still holding him in my arms, and saw that his face was young, but that he had no hair on his head and his features were completely changed. And I said: "I would have known you if I'd met you by chance." And I thought to myself: "Am I telling the truth?" And suddenly I saw him lying like a dead body; then he gradually recovered and went with me into my study carrying a large book of drawing paper. I said: "I drew that," and he answered by bowing his head. I opened the book, and on every page there were beautiful drawings. And in my dream I knew that these drawings represented the love adventures of the soul with its beloved. And on the pages I saw a beautiful image of a maiden in transparent garments and with a transparent body, flying up to the clouds. And I seemed to know that this maiden was nothing other than a representation of the Song of Songs. And looking at those drawings I felt that I was doing wrong, but could not tear myself away from them. Lord, help me! My God, if Your forsaking me is Your doing, then Your will be done; but if I am myself the cause, teach me what I should do! I will be destroyed by my depravity if You utterly desert me!

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The Rostovs' financial situation had not improved during the two years they spent in the country.

Though Nicholas Rostov had stuck firmly to his resolution and was still serving modestly in an undistinguished regiment, spending comparatively little, the way of life at Otradnoe — Mitenka's management of affairs in particular — was such that debts inevitably grew every year. The only obvious course left for the old count was to apply for a government position, so he had come to Petersburg to look for one and also, as he said, to let the girls enjoy themselves one last time.
Soon after their arrival in Petersburg, Berg proposed to Vera and was accepted.

Though in Moscow the Rostovs belonged to the best society without giving it a second thought, in Petersburg their circle of acquaintances was a mixed and uncertain one. In Petersburg they were provincials, and the very people they had entertained in Moscow without asking which set they belonged to now looked down on them.

The Rostovs kept up the same hospitable way of life in Petersburg as in Moscow, and the most varied people gathered at their suppers. Country neighbors from Otradnoe, impoverished old landowners and their daughters, Peronskaya the lady-in-waiting, Pierre Bezukhov, and the son of their district postmaster who had secured a post in Petersburg.
