Among the men who soon became regular visitors at the Rostovs' house were Boris, Pierre whom the count had met in the street and dragged home with him, and Berg, who spent whole days at the Rostovs' and paid the eldest daughter, Countess Vera, the kind of attention a young man shows when he intends to propose.

Not for nothing had Berg shown everyone his right hand, wounded at Austerlitz, while holding a perfectly unnecessary sword in his left. He told that story so persistently and with such an air of importance that everyone believed in the merit and usefulness of his deed, and he received two decorations for Austerlitz.

In the Finnish war he also managed to distinguish himself. He had picked up a fragment of a grenade that had killed an aide-de-camp near the commander-in-chief and brought it to his superior. Just as after Austerlitz, he told this story at such length and so insistently that everyone believed it had been a necessary thing to do, and he received two more decorations for the Finnish war. By 1809 he was a captain in the Guards, wore medals, and held some special lucrative posts in Petersburg.

Though some skeptics smiled when told of Berg's achievements, it couldn't be denied that he was a conscientious and brave officer, on excellent terms with his superiors, and a moral young man with a brilliant career ahead of him and a secure position in society.

Four years earlier, meeting a German acquaintance in the stalls of a Moscow theater, Berg had pointed out Vera Rostova and said in German: "That girl will be my wife" — and from that moment he had made up his mind to marry her. Now in Petersburg, having assessed the Rostovs' position and his own, he decided the time had come to propose.
* "That girl shall be my wife."

Berg's proposal was at first received with a puzzlement that was not flattering to him. At first it seemed odd that the son of an obscure Baltic gentleman should propose to a Countess Rostova; but Berg's defining quality was such an innocent and good-natured self-regard that the Rostovs gradually came around to thinking it would be a good thing, since he himself was so absolutely convinced that it was good — indeed, excellent. Moreover, the Rostovs' finances were in serious trouble, as the suitor surely knew; and above all, Vera was twenty-four, had been taken out everywhere, and though she was certainly good-looking and sensible, no one had yet proposed to her. So they gave their consent.

"You see," said Berg to a friend — he called this man "friend" only because he knew that everyone has friends — "you see, I've thought it all through, and I wouldn't be marrying if I hadn't considered every angle or if it were in any way a bad match. But on the contrary, my father and mother are now provided for — I've arranged that rental property for them in the Baltic Provinces — and I can live in Petersburg on my pay, and with her fortune and my good management we can get along nicely. I'm not marrying for money — I consider that dishonorable — but a wife should bring her share and a husband his. I have my position in the service, she has connections and some means. In our times that counts for something, doesn't it? But above all, she is a handsome, respectable girl, and she loves me..."
Berg blushed and smiled.

"And I love her, because her character is sensible and very good. Now the other sister, though they're from the same family, is quite different — an unpleasant personality and not the same intelligence. She's so... you know?... Unpleasant... But my fiancee!... Well, you'll be coming," he started to say "to dinner," but changed his mind and said "to take tea with us," and quickly curling his tongue he blew a small round ring of tobacco smoke — a perfect picture of his dream of happiness.

After the initial puzzlement at Berg's proposal, the standard festive mood took over the family, but the celebration was outward and forced. In the family's feelings about this wedding there was an unmistakable awkwardness and unease, as if they were ashamed of not having loved Vera enough and of being so eager to get her off their hands. The old count felt this most keenly. He probably couldn't have said what caused his embarrassment, but it came from the state of his finances. He had no idea how much he had, what his debts amounted to, or what dowry he could give Vera. When his daughters were born he had set aside for each of them an estate with three hundred serfs as a dowry; but one estate had already been sold, and the other was mortgaged with the interest so far in arrears that it would have to be sold too, making it impossible to give it to Vera. Nor did he have any money.

Berg had already been engaged for a month, and only a week remained before the wedding, but the count had still not settled in his own mind the question of the dowry, nor spoken to his wife about it. At one time he thought of giving Vera the Ryazan estate, or selling a forest, at another of borrowing money on a promissory note. A few days before the wedding, Berg came to the count's study early one morning and, with a pleasant smile, respectfully asked his future father-in-law what Vera's dowry would be. The count was so flustered by this long-anticipated question that without thinking he gave the first answer that came to mind: "I appreciate your being businesslike about it... I appreciate it. You'll be satisfied..."

And patting Berg on the shoulder he stood up, hoping to end the conversation. But Berg, smiling pleasantly, explained that if he didn't know for certain how much Vera would have and didn't receive at least part of the dowry in advance, he would have to break off the engagement.
"Because, consider, Count — if I allowed myself to marry without definite means to support my wife, I would be acting dishonorably..."

The conversation ended with the count, who wished to be generous and avoid further pressure, saying that he would give a promissory note for eighty thousand rubles. Berg smiled humbly, kissed the count on the shoulder, and said he was very grateful, but that it was impossible for him to arrange his new life without receiving thirty thousand in cash. "Or at least twenty thousand, Count," he added, "and then a note for only sixty thousand."
"Yes, yes, all right!" said the count hastily. "Only excuse me, my dear fellow, I'll give you twenty thousand and a note for eighty thousand as well. Yes, yes! Kiss me."

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Natasha was sixteen and it was the year 1809, the very year she had counted to on her fingers with Boris after they had kissed four years ago. Since then she had not seen him. In front of Sonya and her mother, if Boris happened to come up in conversation, she spoke quite freely about that episode as something childish and long-forgotten, hardly worth mentioning. But in the secret depths of her heart, the question of whether her engagement to Boris was a joke or an important, binding promise tormented her.
Since Boris left Moscow in 1805 to join the army, he had not visited the Rostovs. He had been in Moscow several times and had passed near Otradnoe, but had never come to see them.
Sometimes it occurred to Natasha that he didn't want to see her, and this suspicion was confirmed by the sad tone in which her elders spoke of him.
"Old friends are forgotten these days," the countess would say when Boris was mentioned.

Anna Mikhaylovna had also visited them less frequently of late, seemed to carry herself with particular dignity, and always spoke with pride and gratitude about her son's merits and his brilliant career. When the Rostovs came to Petersburg, Boris called on them.

He drove to their house feeling somewhat nervous. The memory of Natasha was his most poetic recollection. But he went with the firm intention of making clear to both her and her parents that the childhood bond between them could not be considered binding on either side. He had a brilliant social position thanks to his closeness to Countess Bezukhova, a brilliant career thanks to the patronage of an important person whose complete confidence he enjoyed, and he was beginning to plan a marriage with one of the richest heiresses in Petersburg — plans that might very easily come to fruition. When he entered the Rostovs' drawing room, Natasha was in her own room. When she heard of his arrival she practically ran into the drawing room, flushed and beaming with a smile far warmer than mere politeness required.

Boris remembered Natasha in a short dress, with dark eyes shining from under her curls and boisterous, childish laughter, as he had known her four years before; and so he was taken aback when a quite different Natasha entered. His face showed delighted astonishment. This expression pleased Natasha.
"Well, do you recognize your little madcap playmate?" asked the countess.
Boris kissed Natasha's hand and said he was amazed at the change in her.
"How pretty you've become!"
"I should think so!" replied Natasha's laughing eyes.
"And is Papa older?" she asked.

Natasha sat down and, without joining in Boris's conversation with the countess, silently and carefully studied her childhood sweetheart. He felt the weight of that determined and affectionate gaze and glanced at her from time to time.

Boris's uniform, spurs, cravat, and the way his hair was styled were all impeccable and in the latest fashion. This Natasha noticed at once. He sat somewhat sideways in the armchair next to the countess, adjusting with his right hand the spotless glove that fit his left hand like a second skin, and he spoke with a particularly refined pursing of his lips about the entertainments of the highest Petersburg society, recalling with gentle irony their old times in Moscow and Moscow acquaintances. It was no accident, Natasha sensed, that when speaking of the highest aristocracy he mentioned an ambassador's ball he had attended, and invitations he had received from such-and-such dignitaries.

All this time Natasha sat silent, looking up at him from under her brows. This gaze disturbed and confused Boris more and more. He looked toward her more frequently, losing the thread of what he was saying. He stayed no more than ten minutes, then rose and took his leave. Those same curious, challenging, somewhat mocking eyes still followed him. After his first visit Boris told himself that Natasha attracted him just as much as ever, but that he must not give in to that feeling, because marrying her — a girl with almost no fortune — would mean the ruin of his career, while renewing their old intimacy without intending to marry her would be dishonorable. Boris made up his mind to avoid meeting Natasha, but despite that resolution he called again a few days later and began calling often and spending whole days at the Rostovs'. It seemed to him that he ought to have a frank talk with Natasha, tell her that the old days must be forgotten, that despite everything she could not be his wife, that he had no means, and they would never let her marry him. But he couldn't bring himself to do it and felt awkward about broaching the subject. Day by day he became more entangled. It seemed to her mother and Sonya that Natasha was in love with Boris as of old. She sang him his favorite songs, showed him her album, made him write in it, would not let him mention the past — making it clear how delightful the present was — and every day he left in a daze, without having said what he'd meant to say, not knowing what he was doing or why he came or how it would all end. He stopped visiting Helene and received reproachful notes from her every day, yet he continued spending whole days at the Rostovs'.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: One night when the old countess, in her nightcap and dressing jacket, without her false curls and with her thin little knob of hair showing under a white cotton cap, was kneeling on a rug, sighing and groaning as she bowed to the ground in prayer, her door creaked and Natasha — also in a dressing jacket, with slippers on her bare feet and her hair in curlers — ran in. The countess, her prayerful mood shattered, looked around and frowned. She was just finishing her last prayer: "Can it be that this bed will be my grave?" Natasha, flushed and eager, seeing her mother at prayer, suddenly checked her rush, half sat down, and unconsciously stuck out her tongue as if scolding herself. Seeing that her mother was still praying, she tiptoed to the bed and, quickly slipping one bare foot against the other, kicked off her slippers and jumped onto the bed the countess had feared might become her grave. This bed was high, with a feather mattress and five pillows, each smaller than the one below. Natasha jumped onto it, sank into the feather mattress, rolled over toward the wall, and began snuggling under the covers as she settled in, pulling her knees up to her chin, kicking out and laughing almost silently — now burying herself head and all, now peeking out at her mother. The countess finished her prayers and came to the bed with a stern face, but seeing that Natasha's head was covered, she smiled in her kind, gentle way.
"Now then, now then!" she said.

"Mama, can we talk? Yes?" said Natasha. "Now, just one kiss on your neck and another... that'll do!" And seizing her mother around the neck, she kissed her on the throat. In her behavior toward her mother Natasha seemed rough, but she was so sensitive and tactful that however she grabbed her mother she always managed to do it without hurting her or making her uncomfortable.

"Well, what is it tonight?" said the mother, having arranged her pillows and waited until Natasha, after turning over a couple of times, had settled down beside her under the quilt, spread out her arms, and put on a serious expression.
These nighttime visits of Natasha's, before the count returned from his club, were one of the greatest pleasures of both mother and daughter.
"What is it tonight? — But I have to tell you..."
Natasha put her hand over her mother's mouth.
"About Boris... I know," she said seriously, "that's what I've come about. Don't say it — I know. No, do tell me!" and she removed her hand. "Tell me, Mama! Is he nice?"

"Natasha, you are sixteen. At your age I was married. You say Boris is nice. He is very nice, and I love him like a son. But what then?... What are you thinking about? You've completely turned his head, I can see that..."

As she said this the countess looked around at her daughter. Natasha was lying gazing steadily straight ahead at one of the mahogany sphinxes carved on the corners of the bedstead, so that the countess could only see her daughter's face in profile. That face struck her by its peculiarly serious and concentrated expression.
Natasha was listening and thinking.
"Well, what then?" said she.
"You've completely turned his head, and why? What do you want from him? You know you can't marry him."
"Why not?" said Natasha, without changing her position.
"Because he's young, because he's poor, because he's a relative... and because you yourself don't love him."
"How do you know?"
"I know. It's not right, darling!"
"But if I want to..." said Natasha.
"Stop talking nonsense," said the countess.
"But if I want to..."
"Natasha, I am serious..."

Natasha didn't let her finish. She took the countess's large hand, kissed it on the back, then on the palm, then turned it over and began kissing first one knuckle, then the space between knuckles, then the next knuckle, whispering: "January, February, March, April, May. Say something, Mama — why are you quiet? Say something!" she cried, turning to her mother, who was gazing tenderly at her daughter and in that contemplation seemed to have forgotten everything she had meant to say.

"It won't do, my love! Not everyone will understand this friendship dating from your childhood, and seeing him so close to you may harm you in the eyes of other young men who visit us, and above all it torments him for nothing. He may already have found a suitable and wealthy match, and now he's half out of his mind."
"Half out of his mind?" repeated Natasha.
"Let me tell you something about myself. I had a cousin..."
"I know! Kirill Matveich... but he's old."
"He wasn't always old. But here's what I'll do, Natasha — I'll have a talk with Boris. He needn't come so often..."
"Why not, if he wants to?"
"Because I know it will come to nothing..."

"How can you know? No, Mama, don't talk to him! What nonsense!" said Natasha in the tone of someone being robbed of her property. "Well, I won't marry him, but let him come if he enjoys it and I enjoy it." Natasha smiled and looked at her mother. "Not to get married, but just... just so," she added.
"How so, my pet?"
"Just so. There's no need to marry him. But... just so."
"Just so, just so," repeated the countess, and shaking all over, she burst into a good-natured, unexpected, elderly laugh.

"Don't laugh, stop!" cried Natasha. "You're shaking the whole bed! You're terribly like me, just the same kind of giggler... Wait..." and she seized the countess's hands and kissed a knuckle on the little finger, saying, "June," and continued, kissing, "July, August," on the other hand. "But, Mama, is he very much in love? What do you think? Was anybody ever so much in love with you? And he's very nice, very, very nice. Only not quite my type — he's so narrow, like the dining room clock... Don't you understand? Narrow, you know — gray, light gray..."
"What rubbish you're talking!" said the countess.
Natasha continued: "Don't you really understand? Nicholas would understand... Bezukhov, now — he's blue, dark blue and red, and he's square."
"You flirt with him too," said the countess, laughing.
"No, he's a Freemason, I've figured it out. He's fine — dark blue and red... How can I explain it to you?"
"Little countess!" the count's voice called from behind the door. "You're not asleep?" Natasha jumped up, snatched her slippers, and ran barefoot to her own room.
It was a long time before she could fall asleep. She kept thinking that no one could understand everything she understood and everything there was inside her.

"Sonya?" she thought, glancing at the curled-up, sleeping little kitten with her enormous braid of hair. "No, how could she? She's so virtuous. She fell in love with Nicholas and doesn't want to know anything more. Even Mama doesn't understand. It's amazing how clever I am and how... charming she is," she went on, speaking of herself in the third person, imagining it was some very wise man — the wisest and best of men — saying it about her. "She has everything, everything," this man continued. "She is unusually intelligent, charming... and then she is pretty, extraordinarily pretty, and agile — she swims and rides superbly... and her voice! One can honestly say it's a wonderful voice!"

She hummed a snippet from her favorite opera by Cherubini, threw herself on her bed, laughed at the pleasant thought that she would fall asleep immediately, called Dunyasha the maid to blow out the candle, and before Dunyasha had even left the room she had already drifted into another, happier world of dreams, where everything was as light and beautiful as in reality, and even more so because it was different.
The next day the countess called Boris aside and had a talk with him, after which he stopped coming to the Rostovs'.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: On the thirty-first of December, New Year's Eve, 1809-10, an old grandee of Catherine's era was hosting a ball and midnight supper. The diplomatic corps and the Emperor himself were expected to attend.

The grandee's famous mansion on the English Quay blazed with countless lights. Police were posted at the brilliantly lit entrance, which was carpeted with red cloth, and not only gendarmes but dozens of police officers and even the police chief himself stood at the door. Carriages kept pulling away and new ones arriving, with footmen in red livery and plumed hats. From the carriages stepped men in uniforms, decorated with stars and ribbons, while ladies in satin and ermine carefully descended the carriage steps that were lowered for them with a clatter, then walked quickly and silently over the red carpet at the entrance.
Almost every time a new carriage arrived, a whisper ran through the crowd and hats were removed.
"The Emperor?... No, a minister... a prince... an ambassador. Look at the plumes!..." was whispered among the crowd.
One person, better dressed than the rest, seemed to know everyone and identified the greatest dignitaries of the day by name.
A third of the guests had already arrived, but the Rostovs, who were to be present, were still rushing to get dressed.

There had been much discussion and preparation for this ball in the Rostov family, many fears that the invitation wouldn't arrive, that the dresses wouldn't be ready, or that something wouldn't be arranged as it should be.

Marya Ignatevna Peronskaya, a thin and shallow lady-in-waiting at the court of the Dowager Empress, who was a friend and relative of the countess and served as the provincial Rostovs' guide to Petersburg high society, was to accompany them to the ball.
They were supposed to pick her up at her house in the Taurida Gardens at ten o'clock, but it was already five minutes to ten and the girls were not yet dressed.

Natasha was going to her first grand ball. She had gotten up at eight that morning and had been in a fever of excitement and activity all day. All her energy since morning had been focused on making sure they all — she herself, Mama, and Sonya — looked as good as possible. Sonya and her mother had put themselves entirely in her hands. The countess was to wear a dark red velvet dress, and the two girls white gauze over pink silk, with roses in their hair, which was styled in the Greek fashion.

All the essentials were already done: feet, hands, necks, and ears washed, perfumed, and powdered, as required for a ball; the openwork silk stockings and white satin ribbon shoes were already on; the hairdressing was nearly finished. Sonya was ready and so was the countess, but Natasha, who had been bustling about helping them all, was running behind. She was still sitting before a mirror in her dressing jacket, draped over her slender shoulders. Sonya stood ready in the middle of the room, pressing the head of a pin till it hurt her delicate finger, fastening a last ribbon that squeaked as the pin went through it.

"That's not right, that's not the way, Sonya!" cried Natasha, turning her head and clutching at her hair with both hands while the maid who was doing it didn't have time to let go. "The bow is wrong. Come here!"
Sonya sat down and Natasha pinned the ribbon on differently.
"Please, miss! I can't work like that," said the maid holding Natasha's hair.
"Oh, all right! Well then, wait. That's right, Sonya."
"Aren't you ready? It's nearly ten," came the countess's voice.
"Right away! Right away! And you, Mama?"
"I just have my cap to pin on."
"Don't do it without me!" called Natasha. "You won't get it right."
"But it's already ten."
They had planned to be at the ball by half past ten, and Natasha still had to get dressed, and they had to stop at the Taurida Gardens.

When her hair was done, Natasha, in her short petticoat with her dancing shoes peeking out below and wearing her mother's dressing jacket, ran up to Sonya, inspected her, and then ran to her mother. Turning her mother's head this way and that, she fastened the cap and, giving her gray hair a quick kiss, ran back to the maids who were hemming up her skirt.

The cause of the delay was Natasha's skirt, which was too long. Two maids were turning up the hem and hurriedly biting off threads. A third, with pins in her mouth, was running between the countess and Sonya, and a fourth held the entire gossamer garment high on one raised hand.
"Mavra, quicker, darling!"
"Hand me my thimble, miss, from over there..."
"Are you ever going to be ready?" asked the count, appearing at the door. "Here's some perfume. Peronskaya must be tired of waiting."
"It's ready, miss," said the maid, holding up the shortened gauze dress with two fingers and blowing and shaking something off it, as if to demonstrate the airiness and purity of what she held.
Natasha began putting on the dress.
"Just a minute! Just a minute! Don't come in, Papa!" she cried to her father as he opened the door — speaking from underneath the filmy fabric that still covered her whole face.
Sonya slammed the door shut. A minute later they let the count in. He was wearing a blue tailcoat, shoes and stockings, and was perfumed, his hair slicked back.
"Oh, Papa! How wonderful you look! Charming!" cried Natasha, standing in the middle of the room smoothing out the folds of her gauze dress.
"Please, miss — let me," said the maid, who was on her knees straightening the skirt and shifting pins from one side of her mouth to the other.
"Say what you want," exclaimed Sonya in a despairing voice as she looked at Natasha, "say what you want — it's still too long."
Natasha stepped back to see herself in the tall mirror. The dress was too long.
"Really, madam, it's not too long at all," said Mavra, crawling on her knees after the young lady.
"Well, if it's too long we'll tack it up... we'll tack it up in a minute," said the resourceful Dunyasha, taking a needle from the front of her shawl and, still on her knees, setting to work again.
Just then, with soft steps, the countess came in shyly, in her cap and velvet gown.
"Ooh, my beauty!" exclaimed the count. "She looks better than any of you!"
He would have embraced her but, blushing, she stepped aside for fear of being rumpled.
"Mama, your cap — more to this side," said Natasha. "I'll fix it," and she lunged forward so fast that the maids tacking her skirt couldn't keep up and a piece of gauze tore off.
"Oh goodness! What happened? Honestly, it wasn't my fault!"
"Never mind, I'll stitch it up — it won't show," said Dunyasha.
"What a beauty — a real queen!" said the old nurse, appearing at the door. "And Sonya! They're lovely!"
At a quarter past ten they finally got into their carriages and set off. But they still had to pick up Peronskaya at the Taurida Gardens.

Peronskaya was completely ready. Despite her age and plainness she had gone through the same process as the Rostovs, but with less fuss — for her it was all routine. Her aging body was washed, perfumed, and powdered in exactly the same way. She had scrubbed behind her ears just as carefully, and when she entered her drawing room in her yellow dress, wearing her badge as lady-in-waiting, her old maid was just as full of admiring enthusiasm as the Rostovs' servants had been.
She praised the Rostovs' outfits. They praised her taste and appearance, and at eleven o'clock, carefully protecting their hairstyles and dresses, they settled into their carriages and drove off.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Natasha had not had a free moment since early morning and had not once had time to think about what lay ahead of her.

In the damp chill and crowded confines of the swaying carriage, she vividly imagined for the first time what awaited her at the ball — the brightly lit rooms, the music, the flowers, the dancing, the Emperor, and all the brilliant young people of Petersburg. The prospect was so dazzling she could hardly believe it would come true, so completely at odds was it with the cold darkness and cramped interior of the carriage. She grasped what lay ahead only when, after stepping over the red carpet at the entrance, she walked into the hall, removed her fur cloak, and — beside Sonya, with her mother behind them — climbed the brightly illuminated staircase between the flowers. Only then did she remember how she was supposed to behave at a ball and tried to strike the grand pose she considered essential for a girl on such an occasion. But fortunately her eyes began to mist over, she could see nothing clearly, her pulse raced at a hundred beats a minute, and blood pounded in her heart. She couldn't hold the pose — it would have made her look ridiculous — and she moved forward almost fainting from excitement, trying with all her might to hide it. And this was exactly what suited her best. Before and behind them other guests were entering, also talking in low voices and wearing ball gowns. The mirrors on the landing reflected ladies in white, pale blue, and pink dresses, with diamonds and pearls on their bare necks and arms.

Natasha looked in the mirrors and could not pick out her own reflection from the rest. Everything blurred into one brilliant procession. On entering the ballroom, the steady murmur of voices, footsteps, and greetings overwhelmed her, and the light and glitter dazzled her even more. The host and hostess, who had already been standing at the door for half an hour repeating the same phrase to each arrival — "Delighted to see you" — greeted the Rostovs and Peronskaya in the same manner.
* "Delighted to see you."

The two girls in their white dresses, each with a rose in her dark hair, curtsied identically, but the hostess's gaze lingered a moment longer on the slender Natasha. She looked at her and gave her alone a special smile beyond the standard hostess greeting. Looking at her, she may have recalled the golden, irrecoverable days of her own girlhood and her own first ball. The host also followed Natasha with his eyes and asked the count which was his daughter.
"Charming!" he said, kissing the tips of his fingers.

In the ballroom, guests stood crowding at the entrance doors, awaiting the Emperor. The countess positioned herself in one of the front rows of the crowd. Natasha heard and felt that several people were asking about her and looking at her. She realized that those who noticed her liked her, and this helped calm her.
"There are some like us and some worse," she thought.
Peronskaya was pointing out the most important people at the ball to the countess.
"That's the Dutch ambassador, do you see? The gray-haired man," she said, indicating an old man with a profusion of silver-gray curly hair, surrounded by ladies laughing at something he was saying.

"Ah, here she is — the Queen of Petersburg, Countess Bezukhova," said Peronskaya, pointing to Helene, who had just entered. "How gorgeous! She's every bit as good as Marya Antonovna. See how the men, young and old, crowd around her. Beautiful and clever, they say... Prince So-and-so is quite mad about her. But look at those two over there — though they're not good-looking, they get even more attention."
She pointed to a lady crossing the room followed by a very plain daughter.
"She's an incredible match — a millionairess," said Peronskaya. "And look, here come her suitors."

"That's Bezukhova's brother, Anatole Kuragin," she said, pointing to a handsome Horse Guards officer who passed by with head held high, looking over the heads of the ladies. "He's handsome, isn't he? I hear they're planning to marry him off to that rich girl. But your cousin, Drubetskoy, is also very attentive to her. They say she has millions. Oh yes, that's the French ambassador himself!" she replied to the countess's question about Caulaincourt. "He looks like a king! All the same, the French are charming — no one more charming in society. Ah, here she is! Yes, she's still the most beautiful of them all, our Marya Antonovna! And how simply she's dressed! Lovely! And that heavy man in spectacles — he's the universal Freemason," she went on, pointing to Pierre. "Put him next to his wife and he looks like a complete buffoon!"

Pierre, swaying his heavy body, made his way through the crowd, nodding to right and left as casually and good-naturedly as if he were pushing through a crowd at a fair. He was evidently looking for someone.

Natasha looked happily at Pierre's familiar face — "the buffoon," as Peronskaya had called him — and knew he was looking for them, for her in particular. He had promised to be at the ball and introduce dance partners to her.

But before he reached them, Pierre stopped beside a very handsome, dark-haired man of medium height in a white uniform, who was standing by a window talking to a tall man wearing decorations and a ribbon. Natasha immediately recognized the shorter, younger man in white: it was Bolkonsky, who seemed to her much younger, happier, and better-looking than before.
"There's someone else we know — Bolkonsky, do you see, Mama?" said Natasha, pointing out Prince Andrew. "You remember, he spent a night with us at Otradnoe."

"Oh, you know him?" said Peronskaya. "I can't stand him. He's the man of the moment right now. And so proud! Takes after his father. He's hand in glove with Speransky, writing some kind of legislation. Just look how he treats the ladies! There's one speaking to him and he's turned away," she said, pointing at him. "I'd give him a piece of my mind if he treated me like that."
* "He is all the rage just now."

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Suddenly there was a stir — everyone began talking and pressing forward and then stepping back — and between the two rows that parted, the Emperor entered to music that struck up at once. Behind him walked his host and hostess. He walked in quickly, bowing to right and left as if eager to get the first moments of the reception over with. The band played the polonaise that was popular at the time, with its well-known words beginning: "Alexander, Elisaveta, all our hearts you ravish quite..." The Emperor passed on into the drawing room, the crowd surged toward the doors, and several people with excited faces hurried there and back again. Then the crowd quickly pulled back from the drawing room door as the Emperor reappeared talking to the hostess. A young man looking flustered swooped down on the ladies, asking them to move aside. Some women, their faces betraying complete forgetfulness of all decorum, pushed forward at the expense of their dresses. The men began choosing partners and taking their places for the polonaise.

Everyone moved back, and the Emperor came smiling out of the drawing room, leading his hostess by the hand but not keeping time with the music. The host followed with Marya Antonovna Naryshkina; then came ambassadors, ministers, and various generals, whom Peronskaya diligently named. More than half the ladies already had partners and were taking up, or preparing to take up, their positions for the polonaise. Natasha felt that she would be left with her mother and Sonya among a minority of women clustered near the wall who had not been asked to dance. She stood with her slender arms hanging down, her barely formed chest rising and falling evenly, holding her breath, her eyes glittering with fright as she stared straight ahead — ready for either the greatest joy or deepest misery. She wasn't thinking about the Emperor or any of those important people Peronskaya kept pointing out — she had only one thought: "Is it possible that nobody will ask me, that I won't be among the first to dance? Is it possible that none of all these men will notice me? They don't even seem to see me, and if they do, they look as though they're thinking, 'Ah, she's not the one I'm after, so she's not worth looking at!' No, it's impossible," she thought. "They must know how much I want to dance, how wonderfully I dance, and how much they would enjoy dancing with me."

The strains of the polonaise, which had been going on for quite some time, had begun to sound like a sad memory to Natasha's ears. She wanted to cry. Peronskaya had left them. The count was at the other end of the room. She and the countess and Sonya stood there by themselves as if in the depths of a forest amid that crowd of strangers, with no one interested in them, no one wanting them. Prince Andrew passed by with a lady on his arm, clearly not recognizing them. The handsome Anatole stood smiling as he talked to his partner and glanced at Natasha the way one glances at a wall. Boris passed them twice and each time looked away. Berg and his wife, who weren't dancing, came up to them.

This family gathering felt humiliating to Natasha — as if there were nowhere else for the family to talk but here at the ball. She didn't listen to or look at Vera, who was telling her something about her own green dress.

At last the Emperor stopped beside his final partner — he had danced with three — and the music stopped. A concerned aide-de-camp ran up to the Rostovs asking them to stand further back, though they were already practically against the wall, and from the gallery came the clear, precise, irresistibly rhythmic strains of a waltz. The Emperor looked down the room with a smile. A minute passed but no one had begun to dance. An aide-de-camp, the Master of Ceremonies, went up to Countess Bezukhova and invited her to dance. She raised her hand with a smile and placed it on his shoulder without looking at him. The aide-de-camp, an expert in his craft, grasped his partner firmly around the waist and with confident precision started gliding smoothly, first around the edge of the circle, then at the corner of the room he caught Helene's left hand and spun her — the only sounds, aside from the ever-quickening music, being the rhythmic click of his spurs on his quick, nimble feet, while at every third beat his partner's velvet dress flared out and seemed to flash as she whirled around. Natasha watched them and was ready to cry because it wasn't she dancing that first turn of the waltz.

Prince Andrew, in the white uniform of a cavalry colonel, wearing stockings and dancing shoes, stood looking animated and bright in the front row of the circle, not far from the Rostovs. Baron Firhoff was talking to him about the first session of the Council of State that was to be held the next day. Prince Andrew, as someone closely connected to Speransky and involved in the work of the legislative commission, could provide reliable information about that session, about which various rumors were circulating. But he wasn't listening to Firhoff — he was looking now at the sovereign and now at the men who meant to dance but hadn't yet worked up the courage to step into the circle.
Prince Andrew was watching these men, intimidated by the Emperor's presence, and the women who were breathlessly longing to be asked to dance.
Pierre came up to him and caught him by the arm.
"You always dance. I have a protegee here — the young Rostova. Ask her," he said.

"Where is she?" asked Bolkonsky. "Excuse me!" he added, turning to the baron, "we'll finish this conversation elsewhere — at a ball one must dance." He stepped forward in the direction Pierre had indicated. The despairing, dejected expression on Natasha's face caught his eye. He recognized her, guessed her feelings, saw that this was her debut, remembered their conversation at the window, and with an expression of pleasure approached Countess Rostova.
"Allow me to introduce you to my daughter," said the countess, her face flushing.

"I have the pleasure of being already acquainted, if the countess remembers me," said Prince Andrew with a low and courteous bow that completely contradicted Peronskaya's remarks about his rudeness. Approaching Natasha, he held out his arm to take her waist before he had even finished his invitation. He asked her to waltz. That trembling expression on Natasha's face, poised between despair and ecstasy, suddenly broke into a happy, grateful, childlike smile.

"I've been waiting for you so long," that frightened, happy little girl seemed to say through the smile that replaced the threatened tears, as she raised her hand to Prince Andrew's shoulder. They were the second couple to enter the circle. Prince Andrew was one of the finest dancers of his day, and Natasha danced exquisitely. Her small feet in their white satin shoes moved swiftly, lightly, and as if of their own accord, while her face beamed with ecstatic happiness. Her slender bare arms and neck were not classically beautiful — compared to Helene's, her shoulders looked thin and her figure undeveloped. But Helene seemed hardened by a kind of varnish, the residue of thousands of gazes that had appraised her, while Natasha was like a girl exposed for the first time, who would have felt deeply embarrassed had she not been assured that this was absolutely proper.

Prince Andrew liked dancing, and wishing to escape as quickly as possible from the political and intellectual conversation everyone kept directing at him, and wishing also to break through the circle of formality he found stifling under the Emperor's presence, he danced — and he had chosen Natasha because Pierre pointed her out and because she was the first pretty girl who caught his eye. But no sooner had he put his arm around that slender, supple waist and felt her moving so close to him, smiling so near — than the wine of her charm went to his head, and he felt himself revived and rejuvenated. After leaving her he stood breathing deeply, watching the other dancers.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After Prince Andrew, Boris came up to ask Natasha for a dance, and then the aide-de-camp who had opened the ball, and several other young men, so that, flushed and happy, passing off her extra partners to Sonya, she danced without stopping all evening. She noticed nothing of what occupied everyone else. Not only did she fail to see that the Emperor had a long conversation with the French ambassador, or that he was especially gracious to a certain lady, or that Prince So-and-so did this and So-and-so said that, or that Helene was a great success and received special attention from Such-and-such — she didn't even see the Emperor, and only realized he'd left because the ball became livelier after his departure. During one of the merry cotillions before supper, Prince Andrew was her partner again. He reminded her of their first meeting in the avenue at Otradnoe and how she had been unable to sleep that moonlit night, and told her how he had accidentally overheard her. Natasha blushed at the memory and tried to excuse herself, as if there had been something to be ashamed of in what Prince Andrew had overheard.

Like all men who have grown up in society, Prince Andrew enjoyed meeting someone who didn't conform to the standard social mold. And such was Natasha, with her surprise, her delight, her shyness, and even her occasional mistakes in French. With her he was especially careful and tender, sitting beside her and talking about the simplest and most trivial things, admiring her shy grace. In the middle of the cotillion, having completed one of the figures, Natasha, still out of breath, was returning to her seat when another dancer chose her. She was tired and panting and clearly thought of declining, but immediately put her hand gaily on the man's shoulder, smiling at Prince Andrew.

"I'd love to sit beside you and rest — I'm tired; but you see how they keep asking me, and I'm glad of it, I'm happy, and I love everybody, and you and I understand all of it" — and much, much more was said in her smile. When her partner released her, Natasha ran across the room to choose two ladies for the figure.
"If she goes to her cousin first and then to another lady, she will be my wife," said Prince Andrew to himself, quite to his own surprise, as he watched her. She did go first to her cousin.

"What nonsense sometimes enters one's head!" thought Prince Andrew. "But one thing is certain — that girl is so charming, so original, that she won't be dancing here a month before she'll be engaged... Girls like her are rare here," he thought, as Natasha, readjusting a rose that was slipping on her bodice, settled down beside him.

When the cotillion ended, the old count in his blue coat came up to the dancers. He invited Prince Andrew to visit them and asked his daughter if she was enjoying herself. Natasha didn't answer at once but only looked up with a smile that said reproachfully: "How can you even ask?"

"I have never enjoyed myself so much!" she said, and Prince Andrew noticed how her thin arms rose quickly as if to embrace her father and instantly dropped again. Natasha was happier than she had ever been in her life. She was at that peak of bliss where one becomes completely kind and good and cannot believe in the possibility of evil, unhappiness, or sorrow.

At that ball Pierre felt for the first time humiliated by the position his wife occupied in court circles. He was gloomy and distracted. A deep furrow ran across his forehead, and standing by a window he stared through his spectacles, seeing no one.
On her way to supper Natasha passed him.
Pierre's gloomy, unhappy expression struck her. She stopped in front of him. She wanted to help him, to share the overflowing abundance of her own happiness.
"How wonderful it is, Count!" she said. "Isn't it?"
Pierre smiled absently, clearly not grasping what she had said.
"Yes, I'm very glad," he said.

"How can anyone be unhappy about anything?" thought Natasha. "Especially such a fine person as Bezukhov!" In Natasha's eyes all the people at the ball were equally good, kind, and wonderful — people who loved one another, none of them capable of hurting anyone else — and so they all ought to be happy.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: The next day Prince Andrew thought about the ball, but his mind didn't linger on it long. "Yes, it was a very brilliant ball," and then... "Yes, that little Rostova is very charming. There's something fresh, original, un-Petersburg-like about her that sets her apart." That was all he thought about the previous evening's ball, and after his morning tea he set to work.
But either from fatigue or lack of sleep he was in no mood for work and couldn't get anything done. He kept criticizing his own work, as he often did, and was glad when he heard someone arriving.

The visitor was Bitski, who served on various committees, frequented all the societies in Petersburg, was a passionate devotee of new ideas and of Speransky, and was a tireless Petersburg gossip — one of those men who choose their opinions the way they choose their clothes, following the latest fashion, but who for that very reason seem to be the most fervent partisans of all. He had barely gotten rid of his hat before he rushed into Prince Andrew's room with a preoccupied air and started talking at once. He had just heard the details of that morning's opening session of the Council of State by the Emperor, and he spoke of it with great enthusiasm. The Emperor's speech had been extraordinary — a speech only a constitutional monarch could deliver. "The Sovereign said plainly that the Council and Senate are estates of the realm; he said that government must rest not on authority but on secure foundations. The Emperor said the fiscal system must be reorganized and the public accounts published," Bitski reported, emphasizing certain words and opening his eyes significantly.
"Ah, yes! Today's events mark an epoch — the greatest epoch in our history," he concluded.

Prince Andrew listened to the account of the Council of State's opening — which he had awaited so impatiently and to which he had attached such importance — and was surprised that this event, now that it had actually taken place, didn't affect him at all and even seemed quite trivial. He listened with quiet irony to Bitski's enthusiastic account. A very simple thought occurred to him: "What does it matter to me or to Bitski what the Emperor chose to say at the Council? Can any of that make me happier or better?"

And this simple reflection suddenly destroyed all the interest Prince Andrew had felt in the upcoming reforms. He was supposed to dine that evening at Speransky's — "with just a few friends," as the host had said when inviting him. The prospect of dinner in the intimate home circle of the man he so admired had greatly interested Prince Andrew, especially since he had never seen Speransky in his domestic surroundings. But now he felt disinclined to go.

At the appointed hour, however, he entered the modest house Speransky owned in the Taurida Gardens. In the parquet-floored dining room of this small house — remarkable for its extreme cleanliness, almost like a monastery — Prince Andrew, who arrived rather late, found the friendly gathering of Speransky's close associates already assembled for the five o'clock meal. There were no ladies present except Speransky's little daughter — long-faced like her father — and her governess. The other guests were Gervais, Magnitsky, and Stolypin. While still in the front hall Prince Andrew heard loud voices and a ringing staccato laugh — a laugh like one hears on stage. Someone — it sounded like Speransky — was unmistakably erupting in ha-ha-ha's. Prince Andrew had never before heard Speransky's famous laugh, and this ringing, high-pitched laughter from a statesman made a strange impression on him.

He entered the dining room. The entire company was standing between two windows at a small table set with appetizers. Speransky, wearing a gray tailcoat with a star on the breast and evidently still in the same waistcoat and high white stock he had worn at the Council session, stood at the table with a beaming face. His guests surrounded him. Magnitsky, addressing Speransky, was telling an anecdote, and Speransky was laughing in advance at what Magnitsky was about to say. When Prince Andrew entered, Magnitsky's words were again crowned with laughter. Stolypin gave a deep bass guffaw as he munched bread and cheese. Gervais laughed softly with a hissing chuckle, and Speransky in his high-pitched staccato way.
Still laughing, Speransky held out his soft white hand to Prince Andrew.

"Delighted to see you, Prince," he said. "One moment..." he went on, turning to Magnitsky and interrupting his story. "We've agreed that this is a dinner for relaxation, with not a word about business!" And turning back to the storyteller he began to laugh again.

Prince Andrew looked at the laughing Speransky with astonishment, regret, and disillusionment. It seemed to him that this was not Speransky but someone else entirely. Everything that had formerly appeared mysterious and fascinating in Speransky suddenly became plain and unattractive.

At dinner the conversation never paused for a moment and seemed to consist of entries from a book of funny stories. Before Magnitsky had finished one anecdote, someone else was eager to tell something even funnier. Most of the stories, if not about the civil service directly, were about people in government. It seemed that in this company the insignificance of such people was so firmly established that the only possible attitude toward them was amused mockery. Speransky told how a deaf dignitary at the Council that morning, when asked for his opinion, had replied that he thought so too. Gervais gave a long account of an official inspection, remarkable for the stupidity of everyone involved. Stolypin, stuttering, broke into the conversation and began talking heatedly about administrative abuses under the old system — threatening to make things serious. Magnitsky started teasing Stolypin about his passionate tone. Gervais stepped in with a joke, and the talk reverted to its former lively character.

Evidently Speransky liked to relax after his labors and enjoy himself among friends, and his guests, understanding this, tried to entertain him and amuse themselves. But their gaiety struck Prince Andrew as forced and joyless. Speransky's high-pitched voice grated on him, and the incessant laughter felt like a false note. Prince Andrew didn't laugh and feared he was dampening the mood, but no one seemed to notice that he was out of step with the general atmosphere. They all appeared very merry.
He tried several times to join in the conversation, but each time his remarks were tossed aside like a cork thrown out of water, and he couldn't joke along with them.

There was nothing wrong or improper in what they said — it was clever and might have been funny — but it lacked that certain something which is the true spirit of humor, and they weren't even aware that such a thing existed.
After dinner Speransky's daughter and her governess got up. He patted the little girl with his white hand and kissed her. And that gesture, too, seemed unnatural to Prince Andrew.

The men stayed at the table over their port, in the English fashion. In the middle of a conversation about Napoleon's affairs in Spain, which they all agreed in approving, Prince Andrew began to voice a contrary opinion. Speransky smiled and, clearly wishing to steer the conversation away from an awkward turn, told a story that had nothing to do with what they'd been discussing. For a few moments everyone was silent.

After sitting at the table for a while longer, Speransky corked a bottle of wine and, remarking, "Good wine travels in style these days," handed it to the servant and stood up. Everyone rose and, still talking loudly, moved into the drawing room. Two letters brought by a courier were handed to Speransky and he took them to his study. As soon as he left the room, the general merriment stopped and the guests began to converse in a sensible, quiet way.

"Now for the recitation!" said Speransky on returning from his study. "A wonderful talent!" he said to Prince Andrew, and Magnitsky immediately struck a pose and began reciting some humorous French verses he had written about various well-known Petersburg figures. He was interrupted several times by applause. When the verses were finished, Prince Andrew went up to Speransky and took his leave.
"Where are you off to so early?" asked Speransky.
"I promised to go to a reception."

They said no more. Prince Andrew looked closely into those mirror-like, impenetrable eyes and felt that it had been absurd of him to have expected anything from Speransky, or from any of his own activities connected with him, or ever to have attributed importance to what Speransky was doing. That precise, humorless laugh rang in Prince Andrew's ears long after he had left the house.

When he got home, Prince Andrew began thinking about his life in Petersburg during those last four months as if it were something completely new. He recalled his efforts, his solicitations, and the history of his army reform project, which had been accepted for consideration but which they were trying to bury in silence simply because another, much worse proposal had already been prepared and submitted to the Emperor. He thought of the committee meetings Berg was part of. He remembered how carefully and at what length everything relating to form and procedure was discussed at those meetings, and how studiously everything relating to the actual substance of the work was avoided. He recalled his work on the Legal Code, and how painstakingly he had translated articles from the Roman and French codes into Russian, and he felt ashamed of himself. Then he vividly pictured Bogucharovo, his activities in the country, his trip to Ryazan; he remembered the peasants and Dron the village elder, and mentally applying to them the section on Personal Rights he had divided into paragraphs, he was astonished that he could have spent so much time on such useless work.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: The next day Prince Andrew made calls at several houses he had not previously visited, including the Rostovs', with whom he had renewed his acquaintance at the ball. Apart from considerations of politeness that required the visit, he wanted to see that original, eager girl who had left such a pleasant impression on him — this time in her own home.

Natasha was one of the first to greet him. She was wearing a dark blue house dress in which Prince Andrew thought her even prettier than in her ball gown. She and the entire Rostov family welcomed him as an old friend — simply and warmly. The whole family, whom he had formerly judged harshly, now seemed to him to consist of excellent, straightforward, and kindly people. The old count's hospitality and good nature, which in Petersburg came as a particularly pleasant surprise, were such that Prince Andrew could not refuse to stay for dinner. "Yes," he thought, "they are wonderful people who of course have no idea what a treasure they possess in Natasha; but they are kind folk and make the best possible setting for this strikingly poetic, charming girl, so full of life!"

In Natasha, Prince Andrew sensed a strange world completely unlike his own, brimming with joys he had never known — a different world that had already begun to unsettle him in the Otradnoe avenue and at the window that moonlit night. Now this world no longer unsettled him and was no longer foreign; having entered it himself, he found in it a new kind of pleasure.

After dinner, at Prince Andrew's request, Natasha went to the clavichord and began to sing. Prince Andrew stood by a window talking to the ladies and listened to her. In the middle of a sentence he stopped speaking and suddenly felt tears rising in his throat — something he had thought impossible for him. He looked at Natasha as she sang, and something new and joyful stirred in his soul. He felt happy and at the same time sad. He had absolutely no reason to cry, yet he was on the verge of tears. About what? His former love? The little princess? His disillusionment? His hopes for the future? Yes and no. The main thing was a sudden, vivid awareness of the terrible contrast between something infinitely vast and boundless within him and the limited, material thing that he — and even she — actually was. This contrast weighed on him and yet lifted him while she sang.

As soon as Natasha finished, she went up to him and asked how he liked her voice. She asked this and then grew confused, feeling she shouldn't have asked. He smiled, looking at her, and said he liked her singing as he liked everything she did.

Prince Andrew left the Rostovs' late that evening. He went to bed from habit but soon realized he could not sleep. Having lit his candle he sat up in bed, then got up, then lay down again, not at all bothered by his sleeplessness: his soul was as fresh and joyful as if he had stepped out of a stuffy room into God's own open air. It didn't occur to him that he was falling in love with Natasha; he wasn't thinking about her directly, but only picturing her to himself — and as a result, all of life appeared in a new light. "Why do I struggle, why do I toil in this narrow, confined frame, when life — all life, with all its joys — lies open before me?" he said to himself. And for the first time in a very long while he began making happy plans for the future. He decided he must attend to his son's education by finding a tutor and entrusting the boy to his care, then he should retire from the service and go abroad — see England, Switzerland, and Italy. "I must make use of my freedom while I feel so much strength and youth in me," he told himself. "Pierre was right when he said one must believe in the possibility of happiness in order to be happy, and now I do believe in it. Let the dead bury their dead — while one has life, one must live and be happy!" he thought.
